We utilize observations of GWs at 35 km altitude by the Atmospheric InfraRed Sounder (AIRS) on NASA's Aqua satellite to characterize stratospheric GW activity, observations of GWs at 50-55 km by the Cloud Imaging and Particle Size instrument (CIPS) onboard the Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere (AIM) satellite to describe mesospheric GW activity, and MERRA-2 horizontal winds to characterize the strength of the polar vortex.
To characterize TID activity, we use GNSS TEC data generated by the MIT Haystack Observatory, and focus on geographic areas with best data availability (continental US and Europe).
We also focus on the wintertime season in the Northern Hemisphere, when GW activity has a seasonal maximum.
We consider observations during several recent winters in the context of Arctic polar vortex strength.
Our results indicate that the wind system in the stratosphere and mesosphere plays a major role in the propagation of GWs and TID activity.
Most repeatable results are observed during periods of weak polar vortex (sudden stratospheric warmings), when activity in both GWs and TIDs is reduced.
During strong polar vortex conditions, hotspots in stratospheric GWs (35 km) evolve with altitude, are imprinted on the ionosphere over a wide range of latitudes (25-60N) and longitudes.

During some winters, the highest correlations between GWs and TIDs are seen not directly above hotspots in stratospheric GWs, but several tens of degrees westward, and TIDs are particularly strong over the continental US.
This suggests that mesospheric and lower thermospheric winds play a major role in the upward propagation of GWs and in the locations of geographic regions with amplified TID activity.

title: Ionospheric responses from subauroral to equatorial latitudes to prompt storm-time electric fields: scenarios of intense and frequently subtle global impacts

sentences.text: Interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and Interplanetary electric field (IEF) carried by the solar wind plasma can be very dynamic because of varying activities on the sun which produces structures such as Coronal Mass Ejections and High-Speed Streams.

IMF Bz southward turning causing reconnection of magnetic field lines on the dayside imposes an eastward (dawn-to-dusk) electric field which can map into the ionosphere through the equipotential magnetic field lines.
A prompt dawn-to-dusk electric field can penetrate the high-latitude regions shielded by Region-2 currents into lower latitudes.
Therefore, a prompt penetration electric field (PPEF) is expected to cause ionospheric electrodynamical disturbances.
These processes are well established; however, it is relatively less known as to the efficiency and extension of such penetration into the ionosphere from subauroral to equatorial latitudes.
Important storm-time electron density characteristics in these latitudes are often related to electric field effects.

In this study, we present two main scenarios of PPEF effects where the ionosphere exhibits (1) significant perturbations in well-defined density structures including Storm-Enhanced Density (SED) at subauroral latitudes, expansion of equatorial ionization anomaly (EIA) crests, and onset of equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs); and (2) more subtle but surprisingly frequent global impact, contributing to the ionospheric short-term variability on a regular basis.
We utilize the recent intense geomagnetic storm on 28 Feb 2023 to demonstrate scenario (1) where both SED and EPBs developed during an intense PPEF event accompanying a sudden Bz southward turning.

Several minor geomagnetic disturbance events demonstrate scenario (2), where for each disturbed day, more than 10 PPEF episodes with discernable ionosphere disturbances were observed with simultaneous global responses, being much more intense on the dayside but phased-reversed on the nightside.
These analyses used 6000+ globally distributed GNSS receivers, gauzing accurately total electron content (TEC) responses to various PPEF events.

title: Estimation of Spherical Satellite Drag Coefficients in the Upper Thermosphere during Different Geomagnetic Conditions

sentences.text: Satellite drag coefficients are crucial for determining the neutral mass densities that affect spacecraft operations in the thermosphere.
Due to the variability of space environment, uncertainty in the drag coefficient can lead to significant systematic discrepancies in thermospheric density measurements.
Many studies commonly utilize a constant drag coefficient of 2.2 to calculate the neutral density.
However, the drag coefficient may vary throughout the thermosphere due to its dependence on geomagnetic activity and altitude.
Achieving drag coefficient values with sufficient accuracy remains a challenge.

In this study, "Orbital Atmospheric Density Detection Experimental Satellite" referred to as the QX satellite, is first used to estimate spherical satellite drag coefficient with thermospheric factors and space weather conditions.

By utilizing the QX satellite Precise Orbit Determination (POD) and Two-Line Elements (TLEs) datasets, estimates of the spherical satellite drag coefficient can be used to calculate the ballistic coefficient and thermospheric density.
Our findings reveal that the drag coefficient can be estimated using thermospheric temperature, neutral density, geomagnetic activity, and altitude.
At an altitude of ~510 km, the drag coefficients are revised to approximately 2.426, instead of the constant value of 2.2.
Furthermore, the spherical satellite drag coefficient may decrease due to the significant influence of geomagnetic storms on thermospheric density and temperature as geomagnetic activity increases.
These estimates of the drag coefficient can also be applied to reduce discrepancies in deducing the ballistic coefficient.
Consequently, the thermospheric neutral density can be accurately determined using the drag coefficient estimates, compared with the POD-derived density from the Swarm-B satellite.

title: Revisiting the Ionospheric Disturbances over Low Latitude Region of China during Super Typhoon Hato

sentences.text: The ionospheric conditions can be influenced by factors from both above (such as solar flares and geomagnetic storms) and below (including volcanoes, earthquakes, and severe weather disturbances).
To distinguish these sources from ionospheric observations is important for understanding the ionospheric variability and is practically necessary for the ionospheric forecast.
On the day of Typhoon Hato landfall (August 23, 2017), the Total Electron Content (TEC) in the low-latitude region of China experienced a great increase.
It is noted that a weak geomagnetic storm also occurred on the landfall day.
So, to determine the reasons of this enhancement becomes very interesting.
In this study, we revisit ionospheric disturbances using dense Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) stations, ionosondes, space environment and meteorological data.
Our results demonstrate that the primary source of this TEC enhancement is the weak geomagnetic storm rather than typhoon Hato.
Additionally, we analyze several Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances (TIDs) that have different sources during the typhoon period, furtherly clarifying the impact of Hato on the ionosphere.
Through this study, we want to remind the relevant research on determining the source of ionospheric disturbances to be more detailed and comprehensive.

title: FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 observations of ionosphere responses to forcing from Sun to Earth's surface

sentences.text: FORMOSAT7-COSMIC2 Mission is consist of six satellites equipped with GNSS radio occultation payload, in-situ ion density and velocity meters, and RF beacon transmitters.
The constellation launched in June 2019 is situated at the low inclination orbit of 24 degree and the radio occultation observations could cover up to 40 degree latitudes.

As the operational mission takes ~5000 observations of occultations, plus 100% duty cycle of ion measurements, it provides an unprecedented opportunity to observe the three-dimensional ionosphere hourly.
Taking advantage of this special design of the mission, we have discovered several exciting new phenomena during the three year period.

In this presentation, we will show how the minor magnetic storm could create severe ionosphere effects; how the Antartica stratospheric sudden warming oscillated and modify the ionosphere plasma; how the mission help identify the super plasma bubble created by the gigantic volcano eruption.
All these findings are in the context of coupling the ionosphere to the external forcing sources from Sun to the terrestrial surface.

title: The Data-Driven D-Region Model: A Case for a New Option in the International Reference Ionosphere Model

sentences.text: The Data-Driven D-Region model (D3R) calculates a time-dependent solution of electron density profiles based on simplified D-region chemistry from 40 to 130 km.
In addition to ionization profiles generated by extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation, D3R responds to solar energetic protons, auroral precipitation, and solar X-rays.
Observations of the concurrent solar proton event and solar flares of 4-17 September 2017 are used to examine D3R capabilities.
We examine electron density simulation profiles and high-frequency radio signal absorption characteristics through comparisons to electron density profile observations.
We propose that D3R be considered as an option to provide the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) model with D-region profiles during solar x-ray flares and solar proton events.

title: TEC Correlations: Madrigal GNSS Data vs. WACCM-X SD Weimer and IRI-2020 Models during the 2015 St. Patrick's Day Geomagnetic Storm

abbreviations.WACCM-X: Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere and ionosphere extension

sentences.text: This study investigates the correlations of total electron contents (TECs) between observational data and models across a range of geomagnetic latitudes and geographic longitudes during the geomagnetic storm that occurred on St. Patrick's Day, March 17, 2015.
The observational TEC data were collected from the global region using the Madrigal database.

Subsequently, we compared the observed GNSS TEC values with simulated TEC values generated by two empirical models: the climatological models of the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere and ionosphere extension (WACCM-X) specified dynamics (SD) Weimer and the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI)-2020.
We divided the time variations of TEC into zones based on 20-degree geomagnetic latitudes (high, mid, and low), and each 90-degree longitude.
During the quiet phase, TECs predicted by WACCM-X SD Weimer and IRI-2020 tend to lead and underestimate those from the Madrigal GNSS database region.
However, following the storm period (minimum SYM/H index), TECs from both models are higher than those from the Madrigal GNSS.
The results in comparison with localized data in Thailand will be discussed in detail.
Additionally, the observational ionospheric data in other zones will be incorporated for further investigation.

title: GPS Delay Time at Low Latitude During Severe Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: We investigated GPS delay time at low latitude over Chumphon, Thailand by using Total Electron Content (TEC), during the severe geomagnetic storms event on March 24, 2023.
We found that the value of GPS delay time at geomagnetic storm day is more than a quiet day.
The GPS delay time increases on the severe geomagnetic storm day.
The highest GPS delay time is 0.1 ns and the lowest GPS delay time is 40 ns.
After the geomagnetic storm day, GPS delay time backs to the normal at the highest value at 0.3 ns and the lowest value is 50 ns.
As the results, GPS delay time at low latitude during the severe geomagnetic storms increases when compared to the GPS delay time at the quiet day.
Keywords: GPS delay time, TEC, Geomagnetic storm

title: Abnormal response of ionospheric irregularities in the East Pacific region during the great magnetic storm in April 2023

sentences.text: The strongest magnetic storm since the 25th solar activity cycle occurred on April 23-25, 2023, which had a significant impact on the equatorial plasma bubble/equatorial spread F activity, resulting in an abnormal response of ionospheric irregularities from the eastern Pacific to the western coast of the Americas during the recovery phase of magnetic storm.
The irregularities lasted from night to the next day, and even lasted for more than ten hours.
Using ground-based GPS observation data, SWARM and COSMIC2 satellite observation data, the ionospheric irregularities in the region during the recovery phase of strong magnetic storm was analyzed.

The main results indicate that: (1) During the recovery phase of the magnetic storm on the 24th, the Oceania region in the southern hemisphere exhibits significantly enhanced ionospheric irregularities, which lasted from sunset to the next morning (2100-0900LT).

(2) The Hawaiian Islands in the northern hemisphere experienced a prolonged period of weak ionospheric irregularities during the recovery phase of the storm on the 24th, lasting from around midnight to the following afternoon (0100-1400LT).

(3) During the recovery phase of the magnetic storm on the 24th, there were obvious ionospheric irregularities in the western America near the eastern Pacific Ocean, lasting from postmidnight to near the next morning (0100-0900LT).

The ionospheric irregularities showed obvious north-south asymmetry, with a larger range of extension along the magnetic latitude in the northern hemisphere and a longer duration, lasting up to around noon.

(4) SWARM satellite B detected plasma bubbles/disturbance structures near sunset on the 24th (1941-1949LT) and in the morning (0738-0747LT) when crossing the low latitude region of the Eastern Pacific.

When SWARM satellites A and C crossed the low latitude region from the western America to the eastern Pacific, they detected significant plasma disturbances/bubble structures on the next morning (0519-0527LT, 0514-0524LT).
These results are consistent with the ionospheric irregularities observed by ground-based GPS over this region from night to morning.

(5) When different satellites (1-5) of the COSMIC2 constellation crossed the eastern Pacific region on the 24th, strong ionospheric bubbles and their quasi periodic structures are almost always observed, lasting up to 10-14 hours from night to day.

The electric field of the disturbance dynamo during the recovery phase of magnetic storm may play an important role in the generation of nocturnal plasma bubbles and their diffusion towards the daytime.

title: An update of the NET ionospheric model with integration of storm-time memory

sentences.text: The ionosphere is a partially ionized region of the Earth's upper atmosphere that plays a crucial role in a variety of scientific and industrial applications.
In particular, the ionosphere delays the propagation of GNSS signals, and therefore accurate modeling of its plasma density distributions is essential.

The recently developed Neural network model of the Earth's Topside ionosphere (NET) has been shown to reproduce electron densities very well, capturing the effects of various physical phenomena, including the neutral winds, pre-reversal enhancement uplift of the F2-layer, as well as changes in the mid-latitude ionospheric trough.
The initial model parametrization incorporated the SYM-H and Kp geomagnetic indices, which allowed for the inclusion of information about geomagnetic activity.
However, the time progression of the ionospheric response to geomagnetic storms was not initially addressed.

In this study, we discuss additional input parameters and perform sensitivity tests to assess which drivers lead to an improvement in the model performance and to quantify their influence on the model output.

We demonstrate that the model resolves both global negative and positive storm phases and captures smaller-scale patterns consistent with the enhanced action of equatorward thermospheric winds, among other processes.
Furthermore, we describe the extension of the data set used for model training, and outline future plans for the NET model development.

title: Solar Cycle Dependence of NOAA Space Weather Scales

sentences.text: In this study, we examine the relationship between the occurrence numbers of NOAA space weather scales and the maximum monthly sunspot number in each solar cycle: 1976 to 2020 for R and S scales, and 1933 to 2020 for G scale.
For the radio blackouts (R scale), we use X-ray Sensor (XRS) report and flare summary of Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES).
For the solar radiation storms (S scale), we use solar proton events list from NOAA.
For the geomagnetic storms (G scale), we use K_p-index from GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences.
The monthly sunspot numbers are taken from the Solar Influences Data Analysis Center (SIDC).
From our analysis we find that there are systematic relationships between the occurrence numbers of R(scale 3 and 4) and
G(scale 3 and 4) and the maximum monthly sunspot number.

The occurrence number of R3 scale at strong solar cycle is about three times of that at weak solar cycle, and the occurrence number of G3 scale at strong solar cycle is about 9 times of that at weak cycle.
Our work provides a useful guideline for advancing the space weather scales.

title: Estimation of the early CME propagation direction from coronal dimmings with DIRECD

sentences.text: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are solar energetic events involving eruptions of plasma and magnetic fields that have a significant impact on Space Weather.
They can lead to disruptions in technological systems and potential damage to power grids when directed towards Earth.
Traditional coronagraphs positioned along the Sun-Earth line face challenges in accurately monitoring the early evolution of Earth-directed CMEs due to projection effects.
Coronal dimmings, characterized by localized reductions in extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and soft X-ray emissions, serve as crucial indicators of CMEs in the low corona.
These dimmings result from mass loss and expansion during the eruption.
This study introduces a novel method, DIRECD (Dimming InfeRred Estimate of CME Direction), to estimate the early propagation direction of CMEs based on the expansion of coronal dimmings.
The methodology employs 3D simulations of CMEs using a geometric cone model, exploring parameters such as width, height, source location, and deflection from the radial direction.
The dominant direction of dimming evolution is determined, and an inverse problem is solved to reconstruct an ensemble of CME cones at various heights, widths, and deflections.
The 3D CME direction is derived by comparing the CME orthogonal projections onto the solar sphere with the dimming geometry and extent.
Validated through case studies on October 1, 2011, and September 6, 2011, the DIRECD method reveals the early propagation directions of CMEs.
Specifically, the CME on October 1, 2011, predominantly expands towards the South-East, while the CME on September 6, 2011, inclines towards the North-West.
These findings align with previous studies utilizing multi-viewpoint coronagraphic observations.

The study underscores the utility of coronal dimming information for early CME direction estimation, offering valuable insights for space weather forecasting and the mitigation of potential adverse impacts on Earth before observation in the field-of-view of coronographs.

title: Unveiling the Solar-Terrestrial Coupling: How Indian Mars Orbiter and InSWIM Network Tracked High Speed Solar (HSS) Wind Influence on Magnetosphere-Ionosphere

sentences.text: High-speed streams (HSS) are component of solar wind with larger particle velocities flux, especially at near-Earth space environment.
These streams are geoeffective, as when they interact with slower streams, they create a co-rotating interaction region.

This interaction can influence the geomagnetic response of the Earth's Magnetosphere, Thermosphere, and Ionosphere over several solar rotation periods, thus its observation becomes a crucial topic of consideration.
HSS typically originates from coronal holes along open field lines.

In this multi-station and multi-observation study, we mapped the acceleration of HSS particles from coronal holes, their propagation in the interplanetary medium, and their interaction with the magnetosphere, and how that effect might have percolated in the electron densities in low-equatorial ionospheric region, using multiple Radio Science techniques.
We analyzed two-way radio-sounding data transmitted by the Indian Mars Orbiter Mission from May 9th to 19th, 2015, and determined the turbulence regime of solar wind plasma.
The slope of the spectrum at heliocentric distances of 25-35 Rs ranged from 0.2 to 0.4, indicating underdeveloped turbulence corresponding to the High flow streams.
When cross-referenced with coronal EUV images from SDO/AIA, these instances coincided with earth-facing coronal holes on the solar disk.

Particle bulk velocity near the L1 point, as recorded by the ACE satellite, indicated that speeds started increasing from 400 km/s on May 11th-12th, 2015, and peaked at around 800 km/s on May 13th-14th, suggesting the arrival of HSS with a lag of 2.5 days.
Geomagnetic disturbances during the same period were reflected in the dip in DST index values and the rise in the Ap index on May 12th-14th.

GPS data from the InSWIM network station showed two fold increase in Total Electron Content (TEC) values on these disturbed days over low-latitude ionospheric regions in India, specifically in Trivandrum, Bangalore, and Delhi, representing the dip-equator, near low latitude, and near mid-latitude stations respectively.
We will substantiate this effect of external solar wind forcing on earth's ionosphere further in our presentation.
This unique study connects the intriguing science of High-speed stream propagation and its impact on the Near-Earth environment, offering insights from various vantage points in space and ground.

title: Joint analysis with Swarm and ground stations: ionospheric current system and geomagnetically induced currents

sentences.text: Multi-scale measurements arising from the coordination of the magnetic field at Swarm with Cluster, MMS and ground-based arrays can provide information on the connectivity (closure) of field-aligned currents (FAC), ground induced currents (GIC) and the electrojet currents (AEJ).

Previous conjunctions show coherent FA and ground currents in the polar cusp during the main phase of a geomagnetic storm and at near tail local times during substorm activity, at different altitudes.
Mesoscale cusp FACs show vertical scaling, while intense GIC signals can be associated with FACs driven into the ionosphere (via a modified sub-storm current wedge, SCW).

We extend these studies by performing correlation and MVA analyses on Swarm A&C spacecraft, which allows us to obtain FAC directional distributions of local time (MLT) and latitude (MLAT), which can be combined with the AEJ data (also obtained through Swarm products) and the (R1/R2) auroral boundaries, to examine the effects of the level of geomagnetic activity and the electrojet currents.

We compare the results with the dH/dt components (rates of change of the horizontal ground magnetic field) obtained from ground stations to investigate the coupling relationship between: FACs, AEJ and the influence on GICs.

We will also use the above parameters to observe different events at different times and observe the behaviour of the Swarm satellite each time it passes through the auroral zone, both in the northern and southern hemispheres, in order to see how these parameters vary and compare from event to event.
It is expected that these results will contribute to the understanding of the coupling between the ionospheric current system and the ground currents.

title: Preliminary Analysis of Local K-Index Variation on the Magnetic Equator in the Southern Region of Thailand

abbreviations.GISTDA: Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency Public Organization
abbreviations.NICT: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology

sentences.text: Solar activities induce geomagnetic disturbances that affect satellite communication, navigation application, degrade technologies and contribute to the failure of electric power grid systems.
The local K-index serves as a crucial indicator reflecting the intensity of geomagnetic disturbances in space weather forecasts.
Thailand's positioning along the magnetic equator makes it an optimal location for investigating the Earth's magnetic field behavior during periods of solar activity.

The Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (Public Organization) (GISTDA) collaborates with the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) to deploy a fluxgate magnetometer in the southern region of Thailand, situated in close proximity to the magnetic equator.
The collected data provide three components of the Earth's magnetic field.
This study employs Finish Meteorological Institute (FMI) method to analyze the observation data.
The results of the analysis reveal a correlation between the local K-index and Kp-index.
However, it is noteworthy that the K-index slightly exceeded the Kp-index during periods of high disturbance levels.

The distribution of local K-index shows that the geomagnetic storm (K-index≥5) occurred about 7% of total local K-index in 2023 while the strong and severe storm (K-index≥7) occurred 0.27% of total local K-index.

For the further investigation, we plan to upload the data and show the near real time local K-index on the space weather forecast system or "JASPER" developed by GISTDA to study further impacts e.g. local ionospheric irregularities and estimation of ionospheric delays.

title: Drivers of Extreme Geomagnetic Field Variations: Localized Events

sentences.text: Solar wind interaction with the Earth's magnetosphere is a trigger for geomagnetic storms or disturbances that may impact human technology.
Understanding this interaction is one of the top priority challenges in the space weather community.

During geomagnetic disturbances (GMDs), rapid variations in the geomagnetic field can produce intense geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), which can have a detrimental effect on assets such as, power grids, oil and gas pipelines, or communication systems.
In this study, we analyze the solar wind and magnetosphere-ionosphere processes that produce localized geomagnetic field perturbations (dB/dt) on the ground.
A superposed epoch analysis shows a strong correlation between the localized extreme dB/dt structures and solar wind parameters.
In addition, we use multipoint observations to show direct evidence of magnetosphere fast flows driving intense dB/dt on the ground.

title: Intense Energetic Electron Precipitation Caused by the Self-Limiting of Space Radiation

sentences.text: Understanding the dynamics of trapped electrons within the Van Allen belts is crucial for addressing space radiation hazards and improving satellite operational safety.

In our recent work, we have shown how electron flux in the outer radiation belt electron can be capped at a natural limit as a result of the excitation of intense chorus waves, consistently with Kennel and Petschek's (K-P) theory originally proposed in 1966.
These results also suggested that this natural limit may have a significant impact on the rates and locations of intense precipitation in the atmosphere.

This study combines observations from an ensemble of 70 geomagnetic storms, utilizing data from inner-magnetospheric and low-Earth orbit spacecraft, including the Van Allen Probes, POES, GPS, and Arase missions, to investigate the connection between the K-P-related chorus wave enhancements and electron precipitation.

In particular, we show that the K-P flux capping mechanism predominantly affects the newly injected electron population on the dawn side of the magnetosphere during the main phase of magnetic storms, specifically influencing electrons with energies between 30 and 100 keV. These periods of K-P capping are also associated with the elevated chorus activity, which acts to scatter the particles above the limit into the loss cone, and the resulting electron precipitation, as measured by the POES spacecraft.

By combining multi-point satellite data, we further explore the broader implications of such self-limiting processes for geospace dynamics, including energy transport within the highly coupled solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere system.

title: Supersubstorms (SSSs): on their origin, properties and energetics

sentences.text: Supersubstorms (SSSs) are intense auroral zone geomagnetic activity associated with strong westward auroral electrojet currents (SML < -2500 nT).
The nightside SSS onsets and auroral evolution were found to be substantially different than the Akasofu (1964) standard picture of auroral development for "typical" substorms.
SSSs are the primary causes of geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) at the subauroral zone Mäntsälä gas pipeline, Finland, determined from a 21-year data study.
Intense GIC events were sometimes found on the dayside.
The amount of Joule heating on the dayside is found to be equal to that on the nightside.
Cases will be shown where single SSS events caused major (SYM-H < -100 nT) magnetic storms.
By studying interplanetary shock-related SSS events, we have gained new knowledge of the energetics of SSS events.

title: A Proposed Regional Predictive Geospace/Geoelectric Field Product

sentences.text: Adverse effects from severe space weather pose a significant risk to electrical power grids across the globe.

To address this risk, NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) supports an operational Geospace global magnetosphere model, developed at the University of Michigan, that uses spacecraft measurements at Lagrange point L1 to provide short-term forecasts of geomagnetic activity.
Also to address risks to the grid, SWPC provides nowcasts of the geoelectric field driven by ground-based magnetic field observations.

Predicted magnetic fields from the Geospace model can be used in place of the ground-based magnetic field observations across the US and Canada to create a predictive version of the Geoelectric model.

With the development of a coupled Geospace/Geoelectric model, we previously proposed a regional predictive product for the purpose of forecasting hazardous storm-induced geoelectric fields on a regional level within North America.

These predicted geoelectric fields can be used by power grid operators to estimate risk due to geomagnetically induced currents in the grid with 10-30 minutes lead time during enhanced activity intervals.
At the center of the predictive product is a proposed, localized E-field index scale that translates ground-level horizontal electric field magnitudes to a hazard level ranging from 0-9.

We herein demonstrate this product in the form of predictive maps with Geospace output for several geomagnetic storm events and provide initial validation results of the E-field index for the coupled Geospace/Geoelectric model.

title: Design and Development of the Atmospheric Effects of Precipitation through Energetic X-rays (AEPEX) CubeSat mission

abbreviations.AEPEX: Atmospheric Effects of Precipitation through Energetic X-rays
abbreviations.LASP: Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics

sentences.text: Energetic electrons in the radiation belts are one of the most important sources of radiation in near-Earth space and have critical effects on spacecraft operations.
Fluxes of these electrons can be dramatically enhanced during geomagnetic storms by two orders of magnitude or more; subsequently, these fluxes decay back to nominal levels in a few days.
Precipitation into the upper atmosphere is a primary loss mechanism for these electrons, particularly during the decay phase.

Upon impacting the upper atmosphere, these electrons create new ionization in the lower thermosphere, mesosphere, and even the top of the stratosphere, leading to a chemical response that increases NOx and HOx and destroys ozone.

Quantifying loss rates from the radiation belts as well as the global atmospheric impact requires an accurate estimate of the flux, energy distribution, and spatial and temporal distributions of this precipitation.

The Atmospheric Effects of Precipitation through Energetic X-rays (AEPEX) CubeSat mission aims to quantify the flux, energy distribution, and spatial and temporal extent of radiation belt precipitation by measuring the bremsstrahlung X-rays created during the precipitation process.
The key to the mission is a new instrument called the Atmospheric X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (AXIS), which measures hard X-rays between 50 and 300 keV emitted by Earth's atmosphere.

The AXIS instrument is a spectroscopic imager, made possible through the use of off-the-shelf pixelated detector modules, which provide the energy of each photon count, along with coded aperture optics, enabling imaging of precipitation regions with 100 km resolution over a 1000 x 1000 km field-of-view.
The precipitating electron energy spectrum and flux are additionally measured using dual solid-state energetic particle detectors with heritage from the FIREBIRD CubeSat mission.
The electron spectrum can further be used to constrain the inversion from X-ray fluxes to electron fluxes.
The AEPEX spacecraft is a 6U CubeSat built by the University of Colorado Boulder (CU) and the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics (LASP).
The spacecraft structure and bus are custom-designed and built at CU/LASP based on heritage from previous CubeSats such as CSSWE, MinXSS, and CTIM.
The custom bus includes an electrical power system, command and data handling, flight software, and instrument interface electronics, along with custom-designed double-deployable solar panels.
The mission will be launched into a high-inclination orbit to ensure coverage of high latitudes where radiation belt precipitation occurs; launch is currently scheduled for September 2024.

title: New particle detector for radiation belt small satellite fleet from refurbished flight-spares

abbreviations.CORBES: COnstellation of Radiation BElt Survey program

sentences.text: To cover the needs of the COnstellation of Radiation BElt Survey program (CORBES) we plan to reuse refurbished detector modules from the flight spare of the POLAR Gamma-ray Burst (GRB) polarimeter.
POLAR flew onboard the Chinese TG2 Space Laboratory aiming at the polarization detection of gamma rays with energies from about 10 keV to about 1 MeV.
Besides GRB observations, the instrument proved very useful in detecting Solar Flares and observations of enhanced electron environments during geomagnetic storms.
For the CORBES project, we will use one of POLAR's twenty-five detection modules.
Each such module has a detection head made of sixty-four plastic scintillators and dedicated readout electronics (Front End).
Such a detector can be adapted to the new mission requirements undergoing minor changes while its space heritage is still preserved.

Our detector will make a part of the payload for one satellite from a fleet of about ten cube-sat, all equipped with three types of analogous instruments: Magnetometer (MAG), the Search Coil Wave Detector (SCWD), and the High Energy Electron Detector (HEED).
All satellites will be operating simultaneously and located in the same highly elliptic orbit that crosses radiation belts.
After refurbishing, HEED will fulfill the CORBES scientific objective: providing high-time-resolution electron spectra in the Earth's outer radiation belts.
Our instrument consists of a new scintillation detector head based, as previously on plastic scintillators with optimized dimensions.
Its energy sensitivity for electrons will cover the mission-required energies in the range from 0.1 MeV to 4.0 MeV.
The existing readout electronics, consisting of a conventional multi-pad photo multiplier coupled with a dedicated ASIC will remain unchanged.
The detected signals are processed by a low-power FPGA providing a telemetry stream from all pixels with pulse amplitudes above the threshold.
The readout logic also includes coincidence patterns with veto signals.
Such configuration allows for spectroscopic measurements utilizing the dE-E telescope detection technique.
All electronics use COTS components making detector manufacturing affordable.
Before being proved in space onboard TG2, it has been tested and qualified on-ground in the Proton Irradiation Facility (PIF) at PSI.
Both Displacement Damage and Single Event Effects tests were performed on both single components and fully assembled PCBs.
The planned orbit for the CORBES project poses very high levels of radiation and thus large deposited dose values even for a one-year mission duration.
It demands a careful design of additional shielding required to minimize the radiation-posed risks.
Apart from these modifications: detector head - new scintillator geometry and additional shielding, one still needs to modify a High Voltage supply module.
Its main component i.e. the HV DCDC converter has already been tested for radiation hardness.
The whole detector module will easily fit into the L1 satellite volume.

HEED for CORBES will utilize the nuclear telescope detection technique being and provide both particle energies and identification, being able to distinguish between electrons, protons, and gamma rays.
The telescope configuration will also allow for simultaneous multi-angle observations of the radiation belt environment.

title: Development of a forecast model of the outer radiation belt electrons using the XAI

sentences.text: The radiation belt is a region where the Earth's magnetic field traps the most energetic electrons in geospace.
Large flux variations in energetic electron flux are observed during magnetic storms, and prolonged increases in the outer belt electron flux often leads to satellite anomalies.
Forecasting these flux variations is crucial for mitigating risks and is a key aspect of space weather.
We have developed a forecast model for outer belt electron flux variations using a recurrent neural network (RNN) with long short-term memory (LSTM).
For our model, we used electron flux observed by the HEP and XEP instruments onboard the Arase satellite, as well as solar wind parameters.
Moreover, we integrated eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) into our model to investigate the relative contributions of the input parameters.

The XAI analysis revealed that both solar wind speed and the time-integrated southward IMF contribute to flux enhancement, while an increase in solar wind density contributes to the loss of electron flux.

In summary, our developed model, incorporating RNN with LSTM and XAI, enhance our ability to forecast outer belt electron flux variations, contributing to improved space weather forecast and risk mitigation.

title: The RADiation Impacts on Climate and Atmospheric Loss Satellite(RADICALS) Mission

abbreviations.RADICALS: RADiation Impacts on Climate and Atmospheric Loss Satellite

sentences.text: The RADiation Impacts on Climate and Atmospheric Loss Satellite(RADICALS) is a low-Earth orbiting Canadian small satellite mission investigating the transport of space radiation into the atmosphere, and its impact on Earth's climate.

Scheduled for launch in late 2026, the mission will launch into a polar orbit with an integrated payload comprising two back-to-back look direction High Energy Particle (HEP)telescopes, an X-Ray Imager (XRI) to remote sense energetic particle precipitation using back-scattered Bremsstrahlung X-rays, and a boom mounted FluxGate Magnetometer (FGM) and Search Coil Magnetometer (SCM).
Using an innovative Thomson spin-stabilized configuration, the satellite will sample the pitch angle distributions in the spin-plane twice per spin.

The back-to-back HEP look directions allow for a contemporaneous view of the down-going and back-scattered up-going electrons, at the same time as XRI remote-senses the related Bremsstrahlung, and the magnetometers provide in-situ magnetic signatures of a range of plasma waves.

The key measurement of the pitch angle resolved energetic electron precipitation (EEP) and related back-scatter, including a resolved loss cone, will allow a detailed assessment of the energetic particle energy input to the atmosphere.

Measurements of EEP, in addition to measurements of solar energetic particle (SEP) precipitation, will represent a critical data set for assessing the role of space radiation in the climate system, for example through the catalytic destruction of ozone in the middle atmosphere by NOx and HOx.

Accurately quantifying the impacts of this space radiation on climate requires accurate and loss cone-resolved characterization of the flux of these precipitating energetic particles for inclusion into whole atmosphere models.

The RADICALS explorer will also enable research into potentially catastrophic space-weather radiation effects on satellite infrastructure, and assess impacts on space weather-related interruptions to high frequency radio communications including in relation to aircraft operations in polar regions.
Additional cube- and micro-satellite missions, together with the RADICALS, could form a powerful mini--constellation exploring the space weather-climate system.

title: Global Validation of Data‑assimilative Electron Ring Current Nowcast for Space Weather Applications

sentences.text: The electron ring current is an important subject for space weather, as its particles can damage the satellite infrastructure due to surface charging effects.
In this work, we present a global validation of a data-assimilative nowcast of the electron ring current during a geomagnetic storm.
To this end, we utilize the VERB-4D model, a Fokker-Planck based model, capable of simulating the dynamics of the ring current in a convective-diffusive matter.

Our approach uses measurements from both the Van Allen Probes and Arase, leveraging their respective positions - one on the nightside and the other on the dayside - during the strong geomagnetic storm on September 7, 2017.

The unique positioning of the satellites allows us to assimilate Arase measurements into the VERB-4D model on the nightside and subsequently compare the results against Van Allen Probe measurements on the dayside.
The outcomes of this experiment unveil the substantial impact of assimilating data from a single satellite into the VERB-4D model, significantly enhancing its global performance.
Notably, the stand-alone model tends to overestimate the electron flux on the dayside, a discrepancy that is mitigated when Arase measurements are assimilated on the nightside.

This work demonstrates the importance of data assimilation on the prediction capabilities of ring current models and sheds light on future directions, in which data assimilation could be used for parameter estimation for ring current or radiation belt models.

title: Comparison of Radiation Models for Icao Space Weather Services

sentences.text: Under the auspices of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), a space weather information service started on Nov. 7, 2019, and now four global centers, SWPC, PECASUS, ACFJ and CRC operate this service, handing over its responsibilities every two weeks.
The requested information is to ensure stable use of HF communication and GNSS, and to avoid excessive human exposure to radiation.
The products provided by the four global centers would ideally be indistinguishable.
However, in the present status each center uses its own system for space weather nowcast/forecast, which does not guarantee a harmonized information.
This is especially the case of the assessment of radiation doses caused by relativistic solar energetic particle events called ground-level enhancements (GLEs).
For solving this issue, we compared the results of the radiation models used in the four global centers.
We chose a specific event, GLE69 (Jan. 20, 2005) for comparison.
The results show that all models have similar trends, but quantitatively differ from each other.
We discussed the results of analysis and address first ideas on how to solve this issue.

title: Interplanetary shock imaging radio interferometric array based on small satellites

sentences.text: Continuous monitoring of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs) plays a vital role in modelling of CMEs' heliospheric propagation and improving space weather prediction.
The type II radio bursts produced by CME-driven interplanetary shocks provide an opportunity for us to imaging the CMEs through the interferometry technology.
The interplanetary shock imaging radio interferometric array with small satellites program is proposed.

The formation consists of one mother satellite and seven daughter satellites, forming an interferometric array with the equivalent aperture size of 100 km to conduct three-dimensional tomography of CME-driven shock from 0.1MHz to 30MHz.
A coplanar formation is designed to provide dense baseline distributions.
Then, the fuel budgets for formation deployment and maintenance are analyzed.
Besides, GNSS differential positioning is discussed for relative measurement between the mother and daughter satellites.
Finally, radio interferometric imaging simulations are performed to demonstrate the imaging performances.
The proposed interferometric formation will furnish essential insights into the Earth-directed CMEs' propagation and provide critical and unprecedented observation data for space weather forecasting.

title: Progress on the need for an ionospheric T-scale targeting trans-ionospheric radio wave users

sentences.text: The existing NOAA Space Weather Scale for Geomagnetic Storms (G), Radio Blackouts (R), and Solar Radiation Storms (S) serve a number of user groups affected by space weather.
However, user surveys show the GNSS navigation and satellite communication communities are still not well served.

The latter user group relies on trans-ionospheric radio wave propagation that is impacted by the plasma density content (e.g., line-of-sight total electron content; TEC) and structure or irregularities in the plasma.

Plasma density structure can cause amplitude and phase scintillation in the radio wave signals from refraction, or bending, of the waves around ionospheric structure and subsequent interference effects.

The existing G, R, and S Scales are driven, respectively, by real-time observations from ground-based magnetometers for the Kp index, X-ray flux from the GOES satellite, and the solar energetic proton flux also from the GOES satellite.
The need for a reliable consistent data source is fundamental to the operation of a Scale.
For trans-ionospheric radio waves, a reliable, widely available, repeatable, global data source is from dual-frequency GNSS data, either from ground or space-based platforms.

These measurements from either platform can provide estimates of TEC, and indices related to ionospheric irregularities, such as the rate of change of TEC (ROTI), amplitude scintillation (S4), and phase scintillations (????????), for example.
Recently, significant effort has been devoted to determining the relationships between these different indices and combining observations from ground-based and space-based platforms at all latitudes.

Note that the physical processes driving the ionospheric irregularities are likely to be very different in different latitude domains, and during varying levels of geomagnetic activity from quiet to storm.
Only with this concerted observational effort will sufficient data be available in real-time to drive a T-Scale.

As the observational capability matures at all latitudes to characterize the global ionospheric "state", some effort is also being devoted to the possible design of a scale, in terms of defining the index that will determine the scale levels, what those levels will be and their occurrence frequency, the Scale cadence, and how the scale levels will relate to the various trans-ionospheric radio wave user groups.

title: Design of the scale and path forward

sentences.text: The main goal of this panel meeting is to discuss suggestions for defining a new NOAA Ionospheric Space Weather Scale for trans-ionospheric radio wave propagation.

There is an urgent need to complete current space weather scales related to geomagnetic storms (G), solar radiation storms (S), and radio blackouts (R) in HF propagation by a new "T" scale describing disturbances in trans-ionospheric radio wave propagation.

Such a T-scale shall characterize the ionospheric perturbation degree that may seriously degrade the performance of radio signals used in satellite communication, remote sensing radars and global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) for navigation, positioning, and timing.
The meeting should come up with concrete action items how to proceed in elaborating the new scale in particular utilizing the COSPAR initiated platform ISWAT GB-04.

title: Review of available real-time observations

sentences.text: The main goal of this panel meeting is to discuss suggestions for defining a new NOAA Ionospheric Space Weather Scale for trans-ionospheric radio wave propagation.

There is an urgent need to complete current space weather scales related to geomagnetic storms (G), solar radiation storms (S), and radio blackouts (R) in HF propagation by a new "T" scale describing disturbances in trans-ionospheric radio wave propagation.

Such a T-scale shall characterize the ionospheric perturbation degree that may seriously degrade the performance of radio signals used in satellite communication, remote sensing radars and global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) for navigation, positioning, and timing.
The meeting should come up with concrete action items how to proceed in elaborating the new scale in particular utilizing the COSPAR initiated platform ISWAT GB-04.

title: Earth's Geomagnetic Environment—Progress and Gaps in Understanding, Prediction, and Impacts

sentences.text: Understanding of Earth's geomagnetic environment is critical to mitigating the space weather impacts caused by disruptive geoelectric fields in power lines and other conductors on Earth's surface.
These impacts are the result of a chain of processes driven by the solar wind and linking Earth's magnetosphere, ionosphere, thermosphere and Earth's surface.

Tremendous progress has been made over the last two decades in understanding the solar wind driving mechanisms, the coupling mechanisms connecting the magnetically controlled regions of near-Earth space, and the impacts of these collective processes on human technologies on Earth's surface.

Increasingly sophisticated numerical models are able to simulate the magnetospheric response to the solar wind forcing associated with structures like Coronal Mass Ejections, Corotating Interaction Regions, Interplanetary Shocks, etc.

Magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere coupling remains a great challenge, although new observations and sophisticated models that can assimilate disparate data sets have improved the ability to specify the electrodynamic properties of the high latitude ionosphere.
The temporal and spatial resolution needed to predict the electric fields, conductivities, and currents in the ionosphere is driving the need for further advances.

Challenges remain in the ability of models to quantify uncertainties introduced by propagation of solar wind parameters, to account for numerical effects in model codes, and to handle the special conditions occurring during extreme events.
The impacts to technical systems on the ground are highly sensitive to the local electric properties of Earth's surface, as well as to the specific technology at risk.

Current research is focused on understanding the characteristics of geomagnetic disturbances that are important for geomagnetically induced currents, the development of earth conductivity models, the calculation of geoelectric fields, and the modeling of induced currents in the different affected systems.
New understanding should be targeted to accurately quantify solar wind driving, magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere coupling, and the impacts on specific technologies.

The research, modeling, and observations highlighted in this presentation provide a framework for constructing a plan by which the international science community can comprehensively address the growing threat to human technologies caused by geomagnetic disturbances.

title: Characterization of High Energy Proton Events at Mars During SEP Activity and Quiescent Periods

sentences.text: In contrast to Earth, Mars is weakly shielded by its induced magnetosphere, relatively weak crustal magnetic fields, and tenuous atmosphere.

Thus, the space weather impacts and effects on human explorers and supporting infrastructure (communications, power systems, habitat, etc.), both in orbit around and at the surface of Mars, are very different from the terrestrial experience.
Continuing to improve our understanding of the high-energy particle radiation environment at Mars will be important for both scientific and exploration purposes.

For example, charged particle radiation can cause ionization in the lower and middle Martian atmosphere and subsequently alter the atmospheric chemistry and ionospheric structure, thereby affecting communications (e.g., Sanchez-Cano et al., JGR 2019).
At higher energies, the charged particle radiation can pose a clear health hazard for humans in orbit and at the surface.

In this presentation, we will discuss two populations of energetic protons that contribute to the charged particle radiation environment at Mars: 1) solar energetic particle (SEP) protons associated with solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and 2) galactic cosmic ray (GCR) protons that originate from beyond the heliosphere.
Both particle populations are currently observed in orbit by the SEP instrument onboard the MAVEN spacecraft and at the surface by the RAD instrument on the MSL Curiosity rover at the surface.
The first part of our discussion will focus on the energy spectra for > 13 MeV solar protons that we derived from particle count rate data measured by the SEP instrument onboard the MAVEN spacecraft.

These high energy protons penetrated through the MAVEN/SEP housing during large SEP event activity, such as the well-known September 2017 solar storm event (e.g., Lee et al., JGR 2018) and the more recent event in February 2022 (e.g., Khoo et al., ApJ 2024).

With our derived spectra, we can better characterize the high-energy SEP activity seen in orbit at Mars during Solar Cycles 24 and 25, including the determination of SEP event arrival times, peak times, and peak fluxes for a range of incident proton energies.
In addition to SEP events, we will also discuss the GCR proton spectra (E < 1 GeV) that were derived for several quiescent periods observed throughout the solar activity cycle, as part our analysis.

The second part of our discussion will focus on our comparison of the derived energy spectra for higher energy protons with those measured at the surface by the Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD) onboard the MSL Curiosity Rover.
Note that for RAD to detect energetic protons at the surface, their incident energies must be greater than 150-170 MeV in orbit.

To make the comparison, we use the Planetocosmics radiation transport code to propagate these derived high-energy particle fluxes through a model of Mars' atmosphere to produce modeled surface spectra.
This "ground truth" comparison will demonstrate the robustness of our spectra derivation methodology.

title: The March 1940 Superstorm: Geoelectromagnetic Hazards and Impacts on American Communication and Power Systems

sentences.text: An analysis is made of geophysical records of the 24 March 1940, magnetic storm and related reports of interference on long-line communication and power systems across the contiguous United States and, to a lesser extent, Canada.
Most long-line system interference occurred during local daytime, after the second of two storm sudden commencements and during the early part of the storm's main phase.

The high degree of system interference experienced during this storm is inferred to have been due to unusually large-amplitude and unusually rapid geomagnetic field variation, possibly driven by interacting interplanetary coronal-mass ejections.

Geomagnetic field variation, in turn, induced geoelectric fields in the electrically conducting solid Earth, establishing large potential differences (voltages) between grounding points at communication depots and transformer substations connected by long transmission lines.

It is shown that March 1940 storm-time communication- and power-system interference was primarily experienced over regions of high electromagnetic surface impedance, mainly in the upper Midwest and eastern United States.
Potential differences measured on several grounded long lines during the storm exceeded 1-min resolution voltages that would have been induced by the March 1989 storm.
In some places, voltages exceeded American electric-power-industry benchmarks.
It is concluded that the March 1940 magnetic storm was unusually effective at inducing geoelectric fields.

Although modern communication systems are now much less dependent on long electrically conducting transmission lines, modern electric-power-transmission systems are more dependent on such lines, and they, thus, might experience interference with the future occurrence of a storm as effective as that of March 1940.

title: Intense Geomagnetic Storms and Power Grid Anomalies in Poland during the Solar Cycle 24

sentences.text: We focus on the study of intense geomagnetic storms that occurred during the Solar Cycle 24.
These types of storms are typically accompanied by a southward-directed heliospheric magnetic field Bz component and fast coronal mass ejecta.

In our work, using various machine learning techniques, such as self-organizing maps, principal component analysis, or hierarchical agglomerative clustering, we systematically analyze the potential relationships between transmission line anomalies and space weather events.
We also combine our results with the geoelectric field computed for a region of Poland, based on the local magnetometers data utilizing a 1-D layered conductivity Earth model.

title: Geoelectric field modelling for GIC hazard evaluation in Germany's power grid

sentences.text: The hazard posed by geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) to ground-based conductors arises from the induced geoelectric field (GEF) under geomagnetically disturbed conditions.
Here we report on our latest results of modelling the GEF that drives GICs in Germany's high-voltage transmission grid.
We model the GEF from horizontal geomagnetic disturbance (GMD) vectors and co-located 3-D surface impedance matrices under the plane wave assumption on a grid covering Germany.
GMDs are obtained from measurements of INTERMAGNET geomagnetic observatories.
These are freed from station-specific baselines before Spherical Elementary Current System basis functions are fitted to the residuals.
The baselines capture "nonstorm" geomagnetic variability, which is identified considering 1-minute observatory time series since the year 2000.
We also identify the most disturbed days to facilitate the selection of suitable events for GEF modelling.
The surface impedance is calculated from our dedicated 3-D electrical conductivity model "EuSigma".
It particularly takes care of the top layer, which includes land and marine sediments as well as ocean/sea water and provides realistic impedance near the coast.
We perform pointwise comparisons to independent magnetic and electric field measurements and/or magnetotelluric transfer functions at a few locations.
Based on this initial evaluation of the performance of our GEF model, we hope to improve its calibration in the future to produce reliable GIC hazard maps.

title: Development of a Solid State Transformer for HEMP/GMD Common Mode Current Mitigation

sentences.text: A high-altitude electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) or other geomagnetic disturbance (GMD) has the potential to severely impact the operation of electric power grids by introducing low-frequency common-mode (CM) currents.
These currents, which flow through grounded power transformers, can lead to magnetic saturation in the transformer core and significantly deteriorate their performance.
In this work, a solid-state transformer (SST) that can replace susceptible equipment and improve grid resilience to these threats is developed.
An overview of the power electronics and controls architecture required to enable this protection is provided, and the details of a prototype SST hardware design are described.
Finally, the performance of the SST is evaluated in both steady-state and in response to a CM insult.
The SST is shown to be able to successfully respond to this insult, and future research will focus on how the SST can be deployed in the grid to maximize overall resilience.

title: Investigation of Ionospheric Diurnal Double Maxima over Bangladesh

sentences.text: The diurnal double maxima (DDM) patterns in the total electron content (TEC) of the ionosphere have been inves-tigated using multiple station observations over Bangladesh.
The daily TEC changes in the ionosphere are examined using global navigation satellite (GNSS)
TEC data from 2020 to 2022.
Descriptive statistics are involved in examining the monthly and seasonal variation of the occurrence rate of ionospheric DDM.
To identify the possible disturbance sources responsible for ionospheric DDM, different periods are selected for study when DDM is observed at two of the TEC observing stations.
The results show that the occurrence rate is higher in December, January, and February, but a drastic fall occurs in March and April in all three years.
June and July have the second-highest ionospheric DDM incidence rate.
Furthermore, the occurrence rate of ionospheric DDM is higher in winter and monsoon compared to pre-monsoon and post-monsoon.
This study also found that the disturbance storm time (DST) index and the auroral electrojet (AE) magnetic activity index, which are related to ionospheric DDM, show storm and sub-storm signals.

title: Advancing Disturbance-Storm Time Index Forecasting: A Comparative Analysis of Time Distributed CNN and Bi-LSTM Models in Geomagnetic Storm Prediction

sentences.text: Solar wind, consisting of charged particles such as electrons and protons emitted from the Sun's corona, plays a pivotal role in space weather and geomagnetic phenomena when it interacts with Earth's magnetosphere.
Geomagnetic storms, quantified by the Disturbance-Storm Time (Dst) index, have significant implications for various systems, including power grids and communication networks.

This study explores the use of machine learning models, specifically the Bidirectional Long-Short Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) and the innovative Time Distributed Convolutional Neural Network (TD-CNN), for predicting the Dst index.
A comprehensive dataset spanning from 1998 to 2020, incorporating solar wind observations and Dst index measurements, serves as the foundation for model construction and training.
The models' predictive performance is evaluated using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) metrics.
Notably, TD-CNN demonstrates superior accuracy and faster training times compared to Bi-LSTM, making it a promising choice for real-time Dst Index prediction.
This study contributes valuable insights into TD-CNN's potential in space weather forecasting and solar activity analysis.

title: Energy-Efficient Low-Complexity Power Management in Multi-Core RAN Systems

sentences.text: Energy Efficiency is a crucial consideration in 5G and Beyond especially in RAN.
Base Station (BS) in RAN comprising of Distributed Unit (DU), Central Unit (CU) and Radio Unit (RU) consume significant power.
Varying network traffic patterns provides an opportunity to save power during low-traffic periods.
Existing methods are not proactive and lack real-time training capabilities.
In this paper, we propose an intelligent power management method that proactively adjusts the operating CPU frequency of BS units based on predicted core load.
Multi-core processor in BS may have multiple core-groups, each dedicated to different applications having different core loads.
To ensure better generalization and avoid over fitting the prediction model to a single BS, data from multiple BSs are combined at a Central Management Entity (CME).
We derive simple mathematical formulas for core load prediction of each core-group using Reinforcement Learning (RL) at CME.
Subsequently, the appropriate operating CPU frequency for each BS is determined based on the predicted core load of multiple core-groups.
Experiments are conducted using real network traces at RAN Distributed Unit (DU) comprising of core-groups Internet Protocol (IP) & Transport Layer, Radio Link Control (RLC), and Linux applications.
The proposed adaptive Power Management method reduces processor power consumption by around 10% leading to significant cost savings in commercial deployments.

title: A Surrogate Tiny Machine Learning Model of Variational Autoencoder For Real-Time Baseline Correction of Magnetometer Data

sentences.text: Magnetometers play a vital role in geophysics and space weather prediction applications by collecting terrestrial magnetic field data.
They monitor solar-induced geomagnetic disturbances, providing essential insights into predicting space weather effects on technologies such as satellites, power grids, and communication networks.
However, this data often contains inherent background noise, necessitating accurate baseline correction methods.
Traditional correction techniques are robust but computationally demanding and unsuitable for real-time applications.
Recent progress has investigated the utilization of Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) to process magnetometer data in real time, especially when resources are limited.
However, these edge-based ML solutions often lack the robustness of more computationally intensive probabilistic models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs).
This paper introduces a TinyML-VAE surrogate model designed for real-time magnetometer baseline correction.
The surrogate model approximates an implemented VAE's performance while operating within the constrained resources of an edge device.
The new model retains the VAE's uncertainty quantification capabilities by leveraging surrogate modeling techniques, ensuring robustness.
Experimental out- comes have been displayed, illustrating a comparison between the performance of the TinyML-VAE and the benchmark established by the standard VAE.

title: Second Harmonic-Based Approach to Identify a GIC Flow in Power Transformers

sentences.text: Certain parts of the world can experience active geomagnetic disturbances, which trigger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) to flow through grounding circuits into power systems.
Such currents are quasi-dc currents that can have large magnitudes capable of inflecting damage to power system equipment.
Power transformers are among the vulnerable equipment to GIC flows, which can cause harmonic distortion, disruption in reactive power flow, and thermal damage in transformer windings.
Adverse effects of GIC flows can be minimized by developing a fast, accurate, and reliable detection method of GICs.
Such a detection method can support initiating adequate responses to block the GIC from flowing into power transformers.
This paper presents the development and implementation of a method to detect GIC flows in power transformers.
The developed method is based on extracting the second harmonic present in the differential currents.
The proposed GIC detection is experimentally tested using laboratory 3φ transformers, when operated for different GIC flows and loading levels.
In addition, experimental tests are conducted for magnetizing inrush currents and various faults in both sides of tested transformers.
Test results demonstrate fast and accurate detection of GIC flows with minor sensitivity to the value of the GIC, loading level, and/or transformer core type.
In addition, the proposed 2 nd harmonicbased method is found able to accurately distinguish GIC flows from magnetizing inrush and fault currents.

title: Effects of Grounding Impedance on the Second Harmonic Component Produced by GIC Flows

sentences.text: Geomagnetic disturbances trigger quasi-dc currents that flow through grounding circuits into power systems, mostly through power transformers.
Geomagnetically-induced currents (GICs) can cause severe harmonic distortions, disruption in reactive power flow, and/or thermal damage to power transformers.
These adverse effects of GIC flows on power transformers depend on the GIC magnitude, transformer core design, grounding circuit, and winding configuration.
This paper analyzes the effects of grounding circuit designs on the adverse impacts of GIC flows in power transformers.
These effects are analyzed through experimental tests carried out using laboratory 3ϕ, multi-core power transformers.
Experimental tests are performed for several grounding circuit designs for the test power transformers.
Normal, magnetizing inrush, line-to-line, and line-to-neutral fault conditions are conducted for each tested grounding circuit design.

Results of experimental tests show that grounding circuits with low impedance have minor effects on the GIC flows, while grounding circuits with high impedance tend to reduce the magnitude of the GIC.
In addition, test results demonstrate that grounding circuits have little influence on the harmonic distortion (mainly the 2 nd harmonic component) created by a GIC flow.

title: Impacts of Loading Level on Harmonic Distortion in 3ϕ Auto-Transformers During GIC Flows

sentences.text: Geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) are quasi-dc currents that flow through grounding circuits into power systems.
These currents are triggered by geomagnetic disturbance events, and flow into power systems through grounded, power system components, including 3ϕ auto-transformers.

A GIC flow through a 3ϕ auto-transformer can lead to high levels of harmonic distortion in currents, overheating of auto-transformer windings, and significant increase in auto-transformer reactive power demands.
The severity of GIC flow impacts on a 3ϕ auto-transformer can be dependent on the core design, winding configuration, grounding circuit, and GIC current.
This paper discusses possible contributions of loading levels to GIC impacts on a 3ϕ auto-transformer.
These possible contributions are analyzed through experimental tests carried out using a laboratory 3ϕ, multi-core auto-transformer.
Experimental tests are conducted for various GIC flows, where the loading level is varied.
Test results conclude that the loading level of a 3ϕ auto-transformer can influence the harmonic distortion created by a GIC flow.
In addition, test results show that loading level and load power factor have influences on the reactive power demands of a 3ϕ auto-transformer, when experiencing a GIC flow.

title: A Review of the GIC Blocker Placement Problem

sentences.text: Space weather poses a tremendous threat to power systems: geomagnetic disturbances could result in widespread disruptions and long-duration blackouts, including severe damage to system components.
To mitigate their impacts, a handful of strategies exist, with the most promising being the deployment of transformer neutral blocking devices.
The high cost of these devices, however, precludes their installation at all substations; this motivates the development of effective solutions for the cost-effective placement of such devices.

While the current state-of-the-art in blocker placement methods is insufficient to be applied to real-sized power grids, ongoing research continues to increase the size of networks for which the placement problem remains tractable.

Along these lines, the contributions of this paper are two fold: first, a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in blocker placement methods is provided; and second, a complete optimization formulation ─ implemented and benchmarked in an open-source software ─ for the blocker placement problem is presented.

title: Harmonic Distortions in 3ϕ Auto-Transformers Due to Geomagnetically Induced Currents

sentences.text: Geomagnetic disturbances can trigger large geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) to flow into power systems through grounded equipment.
Several studies identify power transformers (with grounded windings) as the main path for GIC flows into power systems.

The flow of a GIC (dominated by a dc component) through grounded windings of a power transformer can lead to severe impacts on its functionality, such as significant increases in its reactive power demands, high levels of current harmonic distortions, and possible thermal damages.
This article presents case studies and analyses of harmonic distortions in 3ϕ power auto-transformers during GIC flows.
Case studies and analyses are conducted using data collected from laboratory experiments.
Analyzed data sets are collected from 3ϕ power auto-transformers with different power ratings, voltages ratings, and core types.
Furthermore, analyzed sets of data are collected for various levels of GIC flows.
Analysis results reveal that the dc component and 2 nd harmonic dominate the 3ϕ currents in grounded windings of tested 3ϕ power auto-transformers over a wide range of GIC flows.
In addition, the 3 rd , 4 th , 5 th , 6 th , 7 th , and 8 th harmonic components are present with low magnitudes.

title: Low-Latitude Indian Ionospheric TEC Variations during Geomagnetic Quiet and Disturbed Days

sentences.text: The Total Electron Content (TEC) of the ionosphere is a significant characteristic of the ionosphere, particularly for satellite navigation systems.
TEC fluctuations in low latitude Indian stations Bengaluru (13°01ʹ02ʹʹ N, 77°34ʹ12ʹʹ E) and Hyderabad (17°25ʹ02ʹʹ N, 78°33ʹ04ʹʹ E) have been discussed from January 2021 to December 2022.
TEC variations are examined and compared monthly and seasonally for geomagnetic quiet days and geomagnetic disturbed days.
Over both locations, the results demonstrate that on disturbed days TEC levels are greater than on quiet days.
Seasonal fluctuations demonstrate that equinox months have the most TEC variation, whereas summer months have the smallest variation.
Furthermore, a correlation analysis is done between solar flux and TEC under both quiet and dynamic geomagnetic conditions at both locations.
It is found that the link between solar flux and TEC is stronger on calm days than on disturbed days.

title: Resistor-Thyristor Geoinduced Current Protection for Power Transformer

sentences.text: It is demonstrated that geomagnetic storms (GMS) can threaten electric power systems both in the Arctic and the middle latitudes of Russia due to the multi-year trend of magnetic pole relocation from Canada toward the Russian Arctic.
The authors outline the key drawbacks of the well-known resistive grounding systems for power transformer neutrals that provide geoinduced current (GIC) protection.
These include the need for various auxiliary electrical equipment to protect the resistor from single-phase short-circuit currents and isolate the neutral from overvoltage.
Some quantitative criteria are proposed for the grounding resistor impedance to limit the GIC to levels that are safe for the power transformer and do not cause its core saturation.
Some requirements for the resistor-thyristor grounding system of the power transformer neutral were put forward considering the restrictions imposed by the regulatory documents for grounding devices.

The authors developed a resistor-thyristor neutral grounding system that automatically switches to the resistive grounding mode when its core is saturated due to GIC and returns to the solid-grounded mode after the GMS ends.

It is shown that, when active components are represented by photothyristors with internal direct overvoltage fault protection integrated into the silicon pattern and silicon power resistors, the resistor-thyristor grounding system can be implemented without auxiliary electrical equipment.

The authors calculated the electrical effects on the power components of the resistor-thyristor grounding system taking into account the rated power and voltage of the power transformer and the degree of phase voltage asymmetry.

title: Protecting Radial Electric Grid from Geoinduced Currents

sentences.text: Possible ways of protecting radial topology electrical grids from the geoinduced currents (GIC) impact are considered, both by operational switching and by including capacitor banks in the neutral of power transformers.
The authors suggest a method for estimating the GIC values in the neutrals of power transformers of an electric grid.
It allows accounting for the direction of the geoelectric field intensity vector and the spatial location of power transformers.
Possible operational switchings to reduce the vulnerability of power transformers of the radial topology electrical grid are considered.
The principle of the capacitive grounding operation is given to protect a power transformer from the GIC effects by switching a capacitor bank into neutral.
The research defines the conditions where using one capacitor bank only may block the possibility of GIC flowing in the neutrals of all power transformers of the radial electric grid.

The article provides the quantitative examples of GIC calculating without capacitive grounding and at the capacitor bank switching, which confirm the possibility of protecting power transformers from the GIC effects using a minimum number of capacitive grounding points.

title: Decoupled, Decentralized, LQR-Based Controls for E3 HEMP/GMD Mitigation on the Power Grid

sentences.text: High altitude electromagnetic pulses (HEMPs) and solar-geomagnetic disturbances (GMDs) both have the potential to impact the reliable operation of the electric power grid.
GMDs, and the low-frequency portion of HEMP insults, introduce currents into the grid that can result in the magnetic cores of large power transformers becoming saturated.
This paper presents a novel approach to HEMP/GMD mitigation, wherein actively controlled voltage sources are utilized to nullify a low frequency EMP insult.
This method is evaluated on several power system case studies, including a single transformer system, a 20-bus system, and a 150-bus system.
Results show that the active mitigation is able to successfully prevent transformer saturation in all cases.

title: Ionospheric Perturbations over the Low-Latitude Indian Region During the Geomagnetic Storm of 26─28 February 2023

sentences.text: The Impact of a severe geomagnetic storm (SYM-H min = -161 nT) on the ionosphere, which occurred on 26-28 February 2023 is studied using a latitudinal chain of six ground-based GNSS observatories in the Indian region.
The effects of positive and negative ionospheric storms accompanying the whole episode of the storm event are highlighted in this work.
