In addition, GIC estimates derived from MT data differ from those based on the two 3D resistivity models by more than 300 A. A statistical analysis based on MT observation sites identifies six high-risk substations, primarily located in the southern North China Plain and the Lvliang Mountains and Taihang Mountains.

title: Simulation of GIC in the North Island of Aotearoa New Zealand Based on Magnetotelluric Measurements

sentences.text: New magnetotelluric (MT) data, combined with older MT data are used to simulate geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) in the power network of the North Island of Aotearoa New Zealand for two geomagnetic storms.

For the May 2024 G5 Gannon Storm, simulations use magnetic field data from two separate locations—the Intermagnet geomagnetic observatory at Eyrewell (EYR) in the South Island of New Zealand, and a magnetometer (OAKS) in the north-west of the North Island which is part of the MANA (Magnetometer Array for New Zealand Aotearoa) network.
All simulations indicate that the largest GIC occur in transformers around Auckland, at Stratford in the west and Redcliff on the east coast.
Simulations for the Gannon Storm using the OAKS magnetic field data match measured GIC at a single transformer at Henderson in Auckland with a peak GIC of approximately 30 A.
In contrast, simulations using the more distant EYR data (>200 km south) produce peak GIC exceeding 100 A in two transformers at Henderson, and over 50 A at Stratford and Redcliff.

Although the EYR simulation yields similar patterns of GIC impact on substations, transmission lines and individual transformers, these values are inconsistent with both the OAKS-driven simulations and the available GIC observations in the North Island.

A significant conductivity contrast between the western and eastern parts of the Northland peninsula identified by the new MT data may be partly responsible for the large GIC in transformers around Auckland.

title: Large, Long-Lasting Mid-Latitude Geomagnetically Induced Currents During a Moderate Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs) are a key space weather hazard to ground-based infrastructure, and can cause mis-operation or even equipment failure.
The solar wind interacts with the Earth's geomagnetic field, causing the magnetic field at ground level to vary with time.
This variability causes GICs in grounded, conducting networks via coupling with the subsurface geology.

Most studies of the hazard focus on short, high amplitude GICs, but long intervals of lower amplitude GIC can also be problematic, representing a rare but known pathway to equipment damage and power failure.
We evaluate an interval in June 2015 where the power network in New Zealand experienced long-duration, steadily increasing GICs across the South Island.
These GICs were up to 20A and lasted approximately 90 min during an otherwise moderate storm interval, while New Zealand was in the dawn sector.
We investigate the magnetospheric cause, attributing them to a possible diversion of the ring current into the ionosphere.

We test the ability of modeling and proxies to capture this hazard, finding that it can be recreated, but is dependent upon the regional geology, and requires detailed knowledge of the network configuration.

We model two hypothetical examples, (a) where the magnetic perturbation is larger and (b) where a different mid-latitude location is exposed, finding that larger currents are possible and that the vulnerability is not unique to New Zealand.
Our case study highlights the limitations of geomagnetic indices, which we show to be vulnerable to influence from such rare mid-latitude phenomena.

title: The Impact of the May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm on TRISAT Orbital Decay: A TLE-Based Analysis With a Lifetime Forecast

sentences.text: The 10─13 May 2024 geomagnetic storm was one of the strongest space-weather events of Solar Cycle 25 and produced a major expansion of the thermosphere, substantially increasing atmospheric drag on low-Earth-orbit spacecraft.

In this study, we quantify the storm-time orbital response of TRISAT, Slovenia's first 3U CubeSat, using publicly available Two-Line Element data, SWARM-C accelerometer measurements, NRLMSIS-2.1 density estimates, and European Space Agency's DRAMA/OSCAR lifetime modeling.
TLE-derived semimajor-axis variations show that TRISAT's orbital decay increased from a pre-storm baseline of about 0.4 km/day to peak values exceeding 1 km/day during the main phase of the storm.
Over 10─13 May, the semimajor axis decreased by approximately 2.5 km.

Independent density-sensitive observations from SWARM-C and empirical thermospheric modeling indicate a storm-time density enhancement of roughly a factor of 2─3, consistent with the observed acceleration of orbital decay.
Lifetime propagation with DRAMA/OSCAR further indicates that the event shortened TRISAT's remaining orbital lifetime by about 1 week over the analyzed interval.

A broader population analysis of low-Earth-orbit satellites shows that the strongest storm-time degradation occurred among low-altitude, high-drag, non-propulsive spacecraft, placing TRISAT within a particularly vulnerable class of small satellites.

These results demonstrate that short-duration geomagnetic storms can produce measurable mission-level consequences for CubeSats, including accelerated orbital decay, reduced lifetime, and degraded orbit-prediction accuracy.
Empirical thermospheric models such as NRLMSIS-2.1 reproduce the overall density enhancement but may underestimate short-term storm variability.

title: Orbital Decay of the Three SNIPE CubeSats During the Super Geomagnetic Storm in May 2024

abbreviations.SNIPE: Small--scale magNetospheric and Ionospheric Plasma Experiment

sentences.text: The Mother's Day (Gannon) geomagnetic superstorm of May 2024 produced extreme thermospheric heating and expansion, resulting in enhanced atmospheric drag on low Earth orbiting (LEO) satellites.

We investigate storm--time thermospheric drag and density variability using three satellites of the Small--scale magNetospheric and Ionospheric Plasma Experiment (SNIPE) 6U CubeSat constellation, complemented by density measurements from Swarm, GRACE--FO, and MSIS 2.1.

Despite operating at nearly identical orbits, SNIPE--B and SNIPE--D experienced significantly different altitude losses during the storm, attributed to differences in effective along--track cross--sectional area arising from different attitude control modes---demonstrating that spacecraft configuration strongly influences drag even for identical CubeSat platforms.
SNIPE--B's drag--derived density shows strong correlation with GRACE--FO measurements, whereas MSIS 2.1 underestimates density near storm peaks.

However, the inter--altitude drag ratio between SNIPE--A and SNIPE--B agrees qualitatively with MSIS 2.1 predictions, suggesting the model captures thermospheric vertical structure under extreme force.
These results demonstrate that publicly available two--line element data, when combined with attitude information, provide a cost--effective method for monitoring storm--time thermospheric density.

Our findings highlight the importance of attitude information in drag analyses and suggest that CubeSat constellations offer significant potential for thermospheric modeling and space weather monitoring.

title: Space Weather Disrupts Low-Latitude Network RTK: Evidence From LSTIDs During June 2025 Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: The geomagnetic storm on 1 June 2025 generated pronounced large-scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (LSTIDs) over China, captured by dense GNSS networks.

It has been unclear whether network real-time kinematic (NRTK) positioning, which relies on spatial interpolation from multiple reference stations, remains effective under such extreme space weather conditions.
This study provides direct observational evidence that links the passage of LSTIDs to the degradation of NRTK performance in a low-latitude region.
We identified strong LSTIDs with amplitudes of ±0.4 TECU propagating equatorward at speeds of 0.3─1.3 km/s and wavelengths of 1,150─1,600 km during the storm's main phase.
These ionospheric gradients disrupted the spatial correlation assumed by the NRTK algorithm, leading to interpolation residuals exceeding 10 cm.
The largest residuals were mainly associated with satellites to the south of the user station, indicating that the LSTID impact may be modulated by satellite azimuth.
As a result, integer ambiguity resolution frequently failed, reducing the horizontal positioning accuracy to the 5─10 cm level.

These findings delineate a complete observation-based pathway from geomagnetic activity to decimeter-level positioning errors, confirming a specific vulnerability of advanced high-precision navigation infrastructure to LSTIDs during space weather events.

title: Auroral Effect on Mid-Latitude Ionospheric Disturbances Over Europe During the Extreme Geomagnetic Storm of 10 May 2024

sentences.text: Large ionospheric disturbances were observed over Europe during the extreme geomagnetic storm on 10 May 2024.
This study analyzes GNSS--derived total electron content (TEC) and all--sky imager data to investigate these disturbances.
Pronounced TEC enhancements, irregularities, and strong gradients were confined to the auroral region above the mid--latitudes.
These anomalies evolved coherently with the equatorward expansion of the optical aurora.
Large--scale TEC disturbances were found to be moving at mid--latitudes with an equatorward velocity of 726 m/s and an amplitude of up to 7 TECU.
These characteristics were indicative of the auroral expansion rather than of large--scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (LSTIDs), which exhibited weaker amplitudes near the auroral boundary.
This finding contrasts with the interpretation of some previous studies on GNSS observations.
This study demonstrates the visualization of the auroral oval at mid--latitudes using TEC and TEC--derived parameters.

title: Variability of dB/dt in the African Sector During Solar Cycle 24-Implications for Geomagnetically Induced Currents

sentences.text: This paper quantitatively characterizes dB/dt peaks at four African equatorial-- and low--latitude stations, along latitudinal and local--time gradients across different phases of selected geomagnetic storms.

We investigate dB/dt response for intense geomagnetic storms, Dst <= -100 nT observed during solar cycle 24 over four stations in the African equatorial to low--latitude region, namely, Addis Ababa (ADIS, mag lat: 0.18°) in Ethiopia, Abuja (ABJA, mag lat: 0.55°) in Nigeria, Yaounde (YAOD, mag lat: -5.30°) in Cameroon, and Medea (MEDE, mag lat: 27.98°) in Algeria.
Furthermore, we determine the equatorial electrojet (EEJ) current using differential magnetometer technique over Ethiopia.
Results show that the dB/dt magnitudes and timings varied significantly with latitude.
The station within the EEJ zone, ADIS exhibited large sharp dB/dt spikes aligned with the EEJ enhancements.
The stations outside the zone (YAOD and MEDE) recorded lower values of dB/dt during the same period, which is consistent with prior studies.
Additionally, fluctuations in dB/dt recurred during the recovery phase, likely influenced by ionospheric currents, substorm activity, and local ionospheric conductivity.
These findings highlight the need to re--evaluate the temporal structure of geomagnetically induced current (GIC) risk in equatorial regions, as hazardous dB/dt.
Enhanced dB/dt values are associated with rapid changes in the solar wind conditions rather than their peak amplitudes.
Higher dB/dt variation does not automatically indicate higher GICs, cautioning GIC practitioners to always isolate natural enhancers of high dB/dt before GIC risk assessments.
Furthermore, this research lays the foundation for the future development of necessary GIC mitigation strategies for Africa.

title: The High-Latitude Workbox for the Ionosphere (HAWK-I): A New Toolkit for Real-Time Specification of the Arctic Ionosphere

sentences.text: The high--latitude ionosphere exhibits rapid spatial and temporal variability during geomagnetically active periods, creating persistent challenges for accurate nowcasts.
The High--latitude Workbox for the Ionosphere (HAWK--I) is a real--time ionosphere nowcast and specification system designed for operational deployment to address these challenges.

HAWK--I employs the Ionospheric Data Assimilation Four--Dimensional (IDA4D) framework, implemented as a three--dimensional variational (3DVar) algorithm, to update a log--electron--density state and produce three--dimensional electron density specifications from GNSS and radio occultation observations at 5--min cadence.
Performance is evaluated during the May 2024 geomagnetic storm using ground--based GNSS Total Electron Content and incoherent scatter radar measurements.

Results demonstrate substantial reductions in TEC error and improved representation of storm--time ionospheric structure relative to background models, with complementary strengths of empirical and physics--based models.

Assimilation of Radio Occulation (RO) observations further improves performance in regions distant from ground--based receivers, highlighting their importance for high--latitude ionospheric specification.

title: Systematic Component-Level Characterization of Electricity Transmission Infrastructure for Space Weather Risk Assessment

sentences.text: Space weather risk assessment is constrained by the lack of available asset information needed to model geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) in electricity transmission infrastructure.
We propose a systematic method that enables risk analysts to collect their own open--source substation data.
Using a web browser platform for annotation, we convert OpenStreetMap (OSM) substation locations into high--resolution, component--level mappings of electricity transmission assets.

We convert an initial 1,313 high--voltage $(\ge 230\ \mathrm{k}\mathrm{V})$ substations to 52,273 components using low--altitude, satellite, and Street View imagery accessed through Google Earth, identifying 7,949 transformers.
Compared to the OSM baseline, this approach provides detailed insights on voltage levels and substation configurations.

We then construct a geospatial GIC network for the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) region, comparing May 2024 results with the University of Illinois Urbana--Champaign 150--bus (UIUC150) synthetic network and with measured ground GICs at 13 monitoring devices.
The transformer types at unannotated substations and the grounding resistances are unknown, so we sample both across a Monte Carlo ensemble.
This gives a median TVA 95th--percentile peak ground GIC of 29.1 A, with a 90% confidence interval of 23.9--36.1 A.

The UIUC150 network yields a 95th--percentile peak ground GIC of 35.8 A under the same forcing, falling within this interval, and the modeled time series broadly capture the temporal morphology of the geomagnetic storm at the monitoring sites.
This method shows promise for spatially explicit, screening--level GIC assessment without requiring access to operator data.

title: Iono-PhyTAU: A Lightweight Global Ionospheric TEC Prediction Model Based on Temporal Attention Unit and Physical Condition Constraints of the Ionosphere

sentences.text: Ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) is the primary error source causing signal delay in Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS).
High--precision TEC prediction is essential for positioning, navigation, and space weather monitoring.

Although deep learning models including ConvLSTM, ConvGRU, and Transformer have advanced TEC forecasting, they still struggle to capture long--range global spatiotemporal dependencies, suffer from severe error accumulation in multi--step prediction, and involve high computational cost and large parameters.
To address these limitations, this paper proposes a lightweight deep learning model called Iono--PhyTAU for global ionospheric TEC prediction.

The model integrates a Temporal Attention Unit (TAU) and external physical driving constraints, which reduces computational complexity, enhances long--sequence dependence modeling, and extracts fine--grained spatiotemporal features.
The model significantly improves TEC prediction accuracy during geomagnetic storms.

Experiments conducted in the high solar activity year (2015) and low solar activity year (2020) show that Iono--PhyTAU achieves the best prediction accuracy, with RMSE values of 2.97 TECU and 1.08 TECU, respectively.

The model effectively alleviates error accumulation in multi--step prediction: after the fourth hr of daily forecasting in 2015, its RMSE is reduced by 0.3--0.5 TECU compared with the suboptimal ConvLSTM model and by 0.5--1.5 TECU compared with C1PG.
In addition, Iono--PhyTAU exhibits strong robustness across different latitudes, seasons, and times, with particularly outstanding performance during geomagnetic storms.
Experimental results confirm that the model can adapt to various space weather environments and performs excellently in geomagnetic storm events.
It has great application potential in improving the reliability of global TEC forecasting and provides strong support for GNSS ionospheric delay correction.

title: Long-Lived Equatorial Plasma Bubbles Persisting Into the Afternoon Over the Pacific Sector During the Recovery Phase of the April 2023 Geomagnetic Storm

abbreviations.ROTI: rate of total electron content index

sentences.text: Equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs) are typically nighttime ionospheric irregularities, and their persistence into daytime sectors remains insufficiently understood.

Here, we investigate long--lived EPB--related plasma depletion structures over the Pacific sector during the recovery phase of the 23--25 April 2023 geomagnetic storm using Formosa Satellite--7/Constellation Observing System for Meteorology, Ionosphere, and Climate--2 (FORMOSAT--7/COSMIC--2) in situ ion density, Swarm--B electron density, ground--based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) rate of total electron content index (ROTI), COSMIC--2 Global Ionospheric Specification (GIS) electron density, and Thermosphere Ionosphere Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics/Global Ultraviolet Imager (TIMED/GUVI)
atomic oxygen--to--molecular nitrogen column density ratio (O/N 2 ) observations.

COSMIC--2 observations show that depletion signatures increased on 24 April, persisted from post--sunrise through local noon, and remained identifiable in the afternoon during 0--6 Universal Time (UT) on 25 April, corresponding to an observable persistence interval of about 20 hr.
Consecutive along--track density profiles reveal that the structures gradually weakened from clear depletions into faint residual signatures while remaining within similar longitude ranges.

Ground--based ROTI observations provide independent evidence for sustained EPB--related irregularities from the postmidnight sector to local noon at the Northern Hemisphere stations and a weaker but longer--lasting response extending into the afternoon at the American Samoa Power Authority (ASPA) station in the Southern Hemisphere.
Swarm--B independently detected a morning super plasma depletion extending to ~35° magnetic latitude in the Southern Hemisphere, corresponding to an apex altitude exceeding ~3,500 km.

COSMIC--2 GIS data show enhanced postmidnight low--latitude topside electron density followed by reduced low--to--middle latitude background density after sunrise, while GUVI O/N 2 observations indicate a hemispherically asymmetric thermospheric composition response.
These observations suggest that the daytime signatures were weak residual traces of storm--time nighttime/postmidnight EPBs rather than newly generated daytime irregularities.

High--apex field--aligned depletion structure and reduced post--sunrise background plasma density likely slowed refilling, enabling residual EPB--related structures to persist into unusually late local--time sectors.

title: Model-Based Analysis of Ionospheric TEC Disturbances Over China and Adjacent Regions During the May 2024 Super Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: This study uses observation data from multi--constellation (GPS/GLONASS/Galileo/BeiDou) ground--based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) networks and a non--integrated spherical harmonic function modeling methodology to develop an ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) model with high spatiotemporal resolution (1° × 1° in longitude and latitude, and 15 min in time) over China and adjacent regions.
The response of regional ionospheric TEC during the May 2024 super geomagnetic storm was then investigated using this model.
The results indicate that the model can accurately capture the spatiotemporal variation characteristics of regional ionospheric TEC during this geomagnetic storm.
During the main and early recovery phases of the geomagnetic storm, positive and negative ionospheric disturbances occurred simultaneously.

During the late recovery phases of the storm, long--lasting negative ionospheric disturbances dominated, causing a substantial TEC decrease, with a maximum decrease of about 70 TECU and a relative decrease of up to 80%.
The daytime ionospheric TEC on 12 May was almost comparable to the typical night--time value.
Additionally, ionospheric response exhibited east--west differences.

Furthermore, during certain periods of the superstorm's recovery phase, positive ionospheric disturbances occurred against an overall negative storm background at middle and low latitudes; this non--locally generated disturbance spans 20°N--40°N with its center near 30°N (projected radius ~10°), propagates westward at ~140 ± 8 m/s, and shows no obvious spatial contraction but a gradual intensity weakening with differential total electron content decreasing from ~30 TECU to 2~3 TECU.
These phenomena indicated that the ionosphere over China and adjacent regions experienced complex variations during this super geomagnetic storm.

title: Feasibility analysis of the Doppler index DI in ionospheric scintillation detection at High Arctic region of Canada

sentences.text: Based on data from 16 ISMR stations of Canadian High Arctic Ionospheric Network (CHAIN)
this study analyses ionospheric scintillation phenomena during the strong geomagnetic storm on April 23, 2023.
The intensity and duration of the geomagnetic storm were confirmed through variations in the Dst and Kp indexes and the global TEC map.
The spatiotemporal distribution and correlation of the DI, ROTI and indexes were analysed, alongside PPP experiments at all stations.
The de-trended TEC (dTEC) analysis revealed a link between ionospheric scintillation and TEC fluctuations.

Statistical results show a correlation coefficient around 0.7─0.9 between the DI index and ROTI/ indexes, with consistent spatiotemporal distributions, especially during the main phase of the geomagnetic storms from 9:00 to 21:00 UTC.

The DI was also applied to explore the impact of ionospheric scintillation on GPS PPP, where the fluctuations in DI corresponded with increased positioning errors, highlighting its effectiveness as a monitoring tool.

title: Application of slant total electron content obtained from the computerized ionospheric tomography for Precise Point Positioning (PPP)

sentences.text: The undifferenced and uncombined precise point positioning (UPPP) method preserves ionospheric parameters as estimable variables, this methodology facilitates the integration of external ionospheric constraints.

In this study, we employ ionospheric tomography technology to obtain high-precision ionospheric products that are applied to UPPP in the forms of slant total electron content (STEC) (PPP-CIT-STEC) and vertical total electron content (VTEC) (PPP-CIT-VTEC).
In addition, the UPPP approach incorporates the 2-dimensional VTEC model (PPP-2D-VTEC).
The positioning performance of these three UPPP methods is compared and analyzed.
Using observation data from the United States and Hunan Province, experiments were conducted for GPS UPPP and BDS UPPP.

The findings revealed that PPP-CIT-STEC significantly outperformed PPP-2D-VTEC and PPP-CIT-VTEC, achieving improvements in positioning accuracy of more than 20% and 12%, and in convergence performance of more than 25% and 13%, respectively.
During the geomagnetic storm, PPP-CIT-STEC also demonstrated remarkable robustness.

This research highlights the efficacy of high-precision ionospheric products in enhancing the performance of UPPP, while also mitigating the influence of mapping functions on positioning outcomes in the computation of ionospheric delays within UPPP.

title: Spectral tracks in the ionosphere: Fast Fourier Transform analysis of seismo-ionospheric coupling through GPS Total Electron Content variations

sentences.text: This study investigates seismo-ionospheric coupling through spectral analysis of Total Electron Content (TEC) variations using a specialized Fast Fourier Transform algorithm (IONOLAB-FFT).
IONOLAB-TEC data from dense GNSS networks are analyzed across thirteen significant earthquakes (Mw 5.6─9.0) in diverse tectonic settings, including nine world events and four in Türkiye.

Consistent spectral patterns are identified retrospectively preceding the earthquakes, characterized by systematic shifts toward lower dominant frequencies, narrowing bandwidths and increasing disturbance durations as seismic events approach.

These patterns show strong magnitude dependence: major earthquakes (Mw ≥ 8.0) exhibit dominant frequencies of 0.3─0.4 mHz with detectable anomalies 4─5 days before the main shock, while moderate events (Mw 6.0─7.0) display higher frequencies (0.7─0.8 mHz) with precursors evident only 1─2 days prior.

Statistical control tests reveal a physically informative asymmetry between the two regional datasets: pre-seismic ionospheric conditions for world earthquakes are statistically indistinguishable from geomagnetically disturbed states, while Türkiye earthquake signals are highly distinguishable from disturbed conditions, particularly in the duration parameter, suggesting different dominant Lithosphere-Atmosphere-Ionosphere Coupling pathways in subduction zone versus shallow crustal tectonic environments.
Long-term time series validation confirms that the identified spectral anomalies represent statistically significant deviations from a stable multi-month ionospheric background.
The consistent patterns observed are observationally consistent with ionospheric responses to pre-seismic strain accumulation, though the underlying physical mechanisms are not directly investigated.

The retrospective nature of the analysis precludes operational application; however, the quantitative multi-parameter framework established here provides a well-defined statistical basis for future prospective validation studies.

title: U-Net Based Forecasting of Storm-Time Total Electron Content over North Africa Using Assimilation of GNSS Observation into Global Ionospheric Maps

sentences.text: This study presents U-Net deep learning of total electron content (TEC) obtained from Global Ionosphere Maps (GIMs) to forecast ionospheric TEC over the African 0─40° N latitude sector during geomagnetic storms which have occurred between 2011 and 2024.

Before being utilized in the deep learning procedure, the GIM-TEC data were improved by assimilating ground-based vertical TEC (VTEC) observations from available Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver stations.
The U-Net one-hour-ahead prediction of TEC was examined during the intense geomagnetic storm of May 2024.
Additionally, the model's accuracy and reliability were evaluated through quantitative comparison with established climatological models, including IRI-2020 and AfriTEC storm time models.
The results indicate that the integration of data assimilation with the deep learning framework yields TEC estimates that closely agree with observations, achieving a RMSE of approximately 5 TECU.
On the other hand, the IRI-2020 model exhibits substantially larger errors, with RMSE ~10─17 TECU, while the AfriTEC model shows the poorest performance, with RMSE reaching approximately 15─22 TECU.

Further, the U-Net was validated using two equatorial and mid-latitude GNSS stations whose data were excluded from the assimilation process, achieving RMSE values of 4.44 and 6.75 TECU and correlation coefficients of 0.93 and 0.97, confirming the model forecasting capability for reproducing ionospheric TEC variability.
These results establish the model as a precise, robust tool for TEC prediction in regions with sparse GPS coverage that is crucial for ionospheric monitoring and space weather applications.

title: Regulatory and Spectrum Challenges for Passive Space Weather Monitoring

sentences.text: Space weather monitoring depends critically on passive sensor systems that detect and measure natural solar and geospace emissions without transmitting radio frequency energy.

These include riometers, solar radio monitors, interplanetary scintillation detectors, GNSS-based ionospheric sensors, and broadband solar spectrographs that enable the provision of critical data required to forecast geomagnetic storms, protect critical infrastructures, and support aviation services, satellite operations, and defense services.

However, with the increasing proliferation of radiocommunication technologies such as 5G/6G networks, dense HF/VHF/UHF deployments, and large constellations of low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, the interference threat to these exceptionally sensitive receivers has grown.
Most of these operate near the thermal noise floor and thus require strict protection criteria to ensure continuity of data.

This review and perspective article provides a cross-disciplinary synthesis of scientific requirements, documented RFI case studies, and ongoing regulatory developments related to spectrum protection for passive space weather sensors.
It systematically integrates perspectives on physical, technical, and regulatory aspects that are typically addressed separately in the literature.

The article reviews the operating principles of major sensor classes and analyzes documented RFI cases affecting GNSS, riometers, CALLISTO, BINGO, and systems impacted by LEO satellite emissions, drawing from existing reports and regulatory submissions.

Building on this evidence base, the work comparatively evaluates regulatory methods under consideration for WRC-27 shows that hybrid approaches combining primary allocations in core observation bands with secondary status and coordination procedures in adjacent bands offer the most viable path forward.
This synthesis contextualizes and analyzes how technical protection criteria can be integrated with existing and evolving regulatory instruments to inform spectrum governance.

The study concludes that without coordinated international spectrum management incorporating explicit protection thresholds and registration procedures, the long-term viability of space weather monitoring infrastructure faces significant risk in an increasingly congested radio frequency environment.

title: Towards Standards in Thermospheric Neutral Density Observation and Validation for Satellite Drag

sentences.text: Discrepancies in neutral density observations present challenges to atmospheric model construction, calibration, and validation efforts.
These discrepancies are often attributed to ballistic coefficient uncertainties resulting from errors in drag coefficients, spacecraft geometries, and masses.
Ongoing progress in drag coefficient physics is poised to reduce the associated sources of errors.
However, the atmospheric modeling community still lacks access to stable, long term, calibration objects with known areas and masses.
Such "standard candles" for satellite drag should span a variety of altitudes and solar cycles to enable comprehensive reanalysis and calibration-validation efforts in the thermosphere.
Their ballistic coefficients should also be stable over those timespans.
Such a list of objects was first presented at COSPAR in 2022.
It is based on a cross-calibration of area-to-mass ratios (AMR) among a population of long-lived resident space objects with stable ballistic coefficients.
The cross-calibration process links space objects with less accurate AMR values with those whose values are well known and published.
In this section of our talk, we will describe the cross-calibration process, its validation, and a means of uncertainty estimation for each AMR value.
We also describe revisions to the original database and its coverage in altitude and time.
Finally, we discuss how the AMR data will be disseminated to the research community.
Another prominent challenge in atmospheric model development is the variety of validation approaches used by the modeling community.
In the context of thermospheric density and satellite drag, such approaches would benefit from harmonization that helps communicate the performance of atmospheric models in an astrodynamics context.
While the thermospheric modeling community has begun to move in this direction with the increased use of log-normal metrics and orbit-effective densities, there is still work to be done.
In this part of the talk, we describe important sources of validation data and how they can be processed to produce "standard" validation metrics.
The talk explores features of these metrics and why they work.
We then discuss potential augmentation of these approaches to better represent astrodynamically meaningful information.
This includes addressing bandwidth (i.e.. temporal coverage) and spatial coverage limitations.
A related aspect of the validation challenge is contextual information for a set of presented metrics.
Too often, a model-data comparison result is shown for a single geomagnetic storm without broader statistical context.
Here the use of a comprehensive standard density reference might be encouraged.
Such a reference has already been produced for the research community in the 20-year density database (2000-2019 ) and is based on the assimilative High Accuracy Satellite Drag Model.
Here, the presentation will demonstrate the benefits of using this reference for model validation.
We also discuss ongoing efforts to expand this database to the present solar cycle.
This expansion will be critical as it also aims to release neutral density forecast archives that will be critical for evaluating progress in the prediction of satellite drag.

title: Auroral activity observed from unusual latitudes in China：insights from CN-DARN observations

sentences.text: Auroras have been observed at unusual latitudes of China over the past couple of years, which may be a direct result of the north magnetic pole's drift and intense solar activity.
However, the specific impact on the Asian space environment remains unknown.

Here, we present auroral activities recorded in southern Inner Mongolia ( 37.2° N in magnetic latitude) and the resulting ionospheric environmental changes detected by the Chinese Dual Auroral Radar Network (CN-DARN) during a recent severe geomagnetic storm.

Leveraging the wide spatial coverage and continuous high time resolution monitoring capabilities of the CN-DARN, comprehensive analysis of ground-based and space-based multi-source data reveals that CNDARN has captured the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of dawnside subauroral polarization streams (SAPS).

The study identifies a direct link between auroral intensification and dawnside SAPS acceleration for the first time, establishing a mechanistic connection between auroral activity and ionospheric convection dynamics in subauroral region.

Moreover, the observations show that the ionospheric irregularities with high velocity of 1,000 m/s induced by the dawnside SAPS have propagated to Mohe ( 48.6° N in magnetic latitude), the northernmost region of China.
The research also reveals that intense auroral particle precipitation caused severe degradation of high-frequency (HF) communications in the Asian region.

This study represents the first comprehensive investigation of auroral activity observed at unusual latitudes of China, unraveling the impact of auroral activities on the ionospheric environment of Asian mid-to-high latitudes.
It also showcases the critical capabilities of the Chinese Meridian Project in addressing space environmental challenges of Asia.

title: Radio-quiet ionosonde measurements for monitoring absorption in the HF band

sentences.text: Enhancements to the D layer of the ionosphere can be produced through different mechanisms: X-ray burst from solar flares or particle impacts due to solar energetic particle events or to auroral precipitation during geomagnetic storms.
Each of these phenomena has a different source, affects a different region and play out on a different timescale.
The final result, however, is in each case an increase in the amount of absorption experienced by HF and VHF radio signals in the ionosphere.
For users of these radio bands, it is important to be aware of the level of D-layer absorption, regardless of which space weather phenomena is ultimately responsible.
There exist several methods to monitor the level of D-layer absorption, but global coverage of observations—especially those available in real-time—is still limited.
We will present a technique to monitor ionospheric absorption in the HF radio band using ionosondes.
This allows us to add real-time absorption data at the location of existing ionosondes, without the need to deploy new instrumentations.
For this purpose, the ionosondes were run in a radio-silent mode, recording not reflections of their own emitted signals but signals from transmitters of opportunity.
Such signals are ubiquitous in all but the most remote, uninhabited regions, especially in various bands reserved for broadcasting applications.
Such bands are intensively used by various users employing relatively high-powered transmitters, which can be received through ionospheric propagation at long distances.
We monitor the signal strength received through the HF band, particularly in the bands reserved for broadcasting, to determine the real-time level of signal attenuation.
We present first the quiet-time data, showing what the typical diurnal patern in the spectrograms is.
This is important as the level of signals received in various bands depends on the location of the observatory.
Absorption can therefore best be determined as a relative variation from the quiet, diurnal variations for a particular location and instrument.
Next, we present the impact of both solar flares and particle storms on the D-layer ionisation, and therefore on the level of absorption of HF radio signals.

We show that solar flares and particle events both have characteristic signatures in the radio-quiet received spectrograms, which allow real-time detection and possibly quantification of absorption enhancements.
We will present several examples observed during the major disturbances that occurred in recent years, as well as the first steps towards a quantification of impacts as a function of frequency.

title: Monitoring of sub-ionospheric VLF/LF signals: Study of radio seismic precursors and solar flares

abbreviations.INFREP: International Network for Frontier Research on Earthquake Precursors

sentences.text: We present recent developments on the investigation of sub-ionospheric VLF/LF signals associated to radio seismic precursors and solar flares collected by the sensors of the International Network for Frontier Research on Earthquake Precursors (INFREP) European radio network consisting of receivers sampling VLF (10-50 kHz) and LF (150-300 kHz) radio signals [2][6].
The radio path distribution allows a continuous monitoring of the lower Earth's ionosphere over central southern Europe.

The Lithosphere-Atmosphere-Ionosphere Coupling (LAIC) model provides explication of radio seismic precursors [7][8] linked to anomalies detected in the VLF/LF radio wave propagation above earthquake regions.
Examples of seismic precursors identified before some of the most recent earthquakes occurred in the Mediterranean region have been reported in [1][3][4][9].
A key step of this analysis is disentangling between seismic and solar contributions at the origin of observed anomalies in the VLF/LF propagation.

Time segments ± 2h around midnight are considered, to get rid of dayside solar driven influences in conjunction with the D-layer ionosphere and to mitigate the strong transitions around the terminators.
The European Severe Weather Database (ESWD) is referred for severe weather events over the region of interest and the GOES satellite data are used to check the occurrence of solar flares.

Besides the study of radio seismic precursors, the impact of strong events from the current solar cycle 25, e.g., x-ray flares and related particle outbursts, on electric field amplitude and phase variations between narrowband VLF/LF transmitters and receivers are analysed.
Complementary measurements collected by muon detectors at the measurement facility of Belgrade, Serbia, are taken into account.
The joint analysis of these two complementary datasets allows a better characterization of single events and the estimation of statistical parameters.
The influence of initial D-layer plasma conditions on modelling ionospheric parameters during a X-ray flare is explained by the Quiet Ionospheric D-Region (QIonDR) model
The Faraday-International Reference Ionosphere (FIRI) semiempirical model is used to calculate the electron densities in an altitude range h = 60─150 km

Results from the study of 86 X-class solar ﬂares (47 events daytime) from 71 days in the period from July 2021 to June 2025 are presented, based on the data collected at the INFREP receiver located in Graz, Austria.
The used VLF signals propagate from the transmitting stations DHO (Germany), ICV, ITS (Italy) and TBB (Turkey).
Changes in the amplitude of VLF signal is compared to the solar flux measured by the GOES satellites.

title: Lithosphere-Atmosphere-Ionosphere coupling of large earthquakes and intense magnetic storms from ASI's CSES Limadou Mission in August 2018

sentences.text: A sun-synchronous satellite, the China seismo-electromagnetic satellite (CSES, also named ZhangHeng-1), orbiting at 507 km altitude with ascending/descending node time of 02:00/14:00 LT, was launched on 2 February 2018 to detect pre-earthquake ionospheric anomalies (PEIAs) and to study space weather effects in the ionosphere.
Since satellite observations provide global and uniform coverage, they are ideally used to observe ionospheric weather and PEIAs.
The CSES probes manifest longitudinal features of 4-peak plasma density and three plasma depletions in the equatorial/low-latitudes as well as mid-latitude troughs.

CSES plasma and the total electron content (TEC) derived from worldwide ground-based GNSS (global navigation satellite system) of the global ionosphere map (GIM) are used to study PEIAs associated with a destructive M7.0 earthquake and its followed M6.5 and M6.3/M6.9 earthquakes in Lombok, Indonesia, on 5, 17, and 19 August 2018, respectively, as well as to examine ionospheric disturbances induced by an intense storm with the Dst index of -175 nT on 26 August 2018.

Anomalous increases (decreases) in the GIM TEC and CSES plasma density (temperature) frequently appear specifically over the epicenter day 1-5 before the M7.0 earthquake and followed earthquakes, when the geomagnetic conditions of these PEIA periods are relatively quiet, Dst: -37 19 nT.
In contrast, TEC and CSES anomalies occur globally in the southern hemisphere during the storm days of 26-28 August 2018.

The CSES ion velocity shows that the electric field of PEIAs associated with the M7.0 earthquake is 0.21 mV/m eastward on 1-3 August 2018, while the penetration electric fields during the storm periods of 26-28 August 2018 are 0.17/0.60 mV/m westward/downward at post-midnight of 02:00 LT and 0.26/0.34 mV/m eastward/upward at post-noon of 14:00 LT.
Spatial analyses on CSES plasma discriminate PEIAs from global effects and locate the epicenter of possible forthcoming large earthquakes.
CSES ion velocities are useful to derive PEIA- and storm-related electric fields in the ionosphere.

Meanwhile, PEIAs associated with the 2008 M8.0 Wenchuan earthquake, the 2017 M7.3 Iran─Iraq border earthquake, and the 2025 M 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake observed DEMETER, FORMOSAT-5, FORMOSAT-7 satellites are reported, respectively.
These results show that the seismo-generated electric field via the lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling plays an important role to induce PEIAs.

title: Response of global low-latitude ionospheric irregularities during the intense magnetic storm in May 2024

sentences.text: The strongest magnetic storm since the 25th solar cycle occurred from May 10 to 14, 2024.
The storm began abruptly at 14 UT on the 10th, with a rapid and slight increase in the Dst index.
The main phase of the storm began at 17 UT, and the Dst index rapidly decreased, reaching a minimum of -406 nT at 02 UT on the 11th.
Subsequently, the recovery phase of the storm began, and the Dst index gradually recovered.
By around 20 UT on the 13th, the Dst index had returned to a level above -50
nT.
The Dst index was below -100 nT from 20 UT on the 10th to 14 UT on the 12th, lasting for 38 hours, during which the Kp index reached a maximum of 9^09^09^0.

Using observational data from the COSMIC-2 and SWARM satellites, as well as ground-based GPS observations, an analysis was conducted on the response of global low-latitude ionospheric irregularities during this intense magnetic storm.
The main results indicate that: (1) Before the occurrence of the magnetic storm, low-latitude ionospheric irregularities mainly occurred in the African region (0^∘∼60^∘).
The occurrence of the magnetic storm had significantly different impacts on ionospheric irregularities in different longitude regions.

(2) During the main phase of the storm on the 10th, a large spatial range of plasma depletion structures appeared at night in the South American-African region (-60^∘∼60^∘), accompanied by ionospheric irregularities, with the most pronounced effects in the African region.
(3) During the recovery phase of the magnetic storm on the 11th, the ionospheric irregularities in the African and Indian Ocean regions (0^∘∼100^∘) almost completely disappeared.
However, in most other longitude regions, there were obvious large-scale plasma depletion structures and enhanced ionospheric irregularity activities.

This was most pronounced in the eastern Pacific region (-180^∘ ∼-60^∘) and the western Pacific region (100^∘∼180^∘), where ionospheric irregularity activities persisted throughout the night and even into the day.

(4) During the recovery phase of the magnetic storm on the 12th and 13th, the South America-Atlantic region (-60^∘∼0^∘) still exhibited large-scale plasma depletion structures and ionospheric irregularity activities.
The ionospheric irregularity activities in the eastern Pacific region gradually weakened, while those in the western Pacific region almost completely disappeared.

The combined effects of the prompt penetration electric field and the disturbance dynamo electric field during the magnetic storm may play an important role in generating/suppressing ionospheric irregularity activities in different low-latitude regions.

title: Physical Constraints on the Occurrence of Super Plasma Bubbles over the American Sector

abbreviations.ROTI: Rate of Total Electron Content Index

sentences.text: Super plasma bubbles (SPBs) are intense plasma density depletions in the ionospheric F region that extend far beyond their usual equatorial domain and occur predominantly during geomagnetic storms.

Although magnetic declination is known to modulate the seasonal occurrence and morphology of plasma bubbles under quiet-time conditions, the physical constraints governing the occurrence of SPBs, particularly during geomagnetically disturbed periods, remain poorly understood.

In this study, we investigate the common physical conditions associated with the occurrence and longitudinal localization of SPBs over the American sector by analyzing a sequence of intense geomagnetic storms during which SPBs were observed on 1 June 2013, 27 May 2017, 7 September 2017, 10 October 2024, and 12 November 2025.

We employ a multi-instrument data set including Rate of Total Electron Content Index (ROTI) maps derived from approximately 2,800 ground-based GNSS receivers, ionosonde observations from a regional network, all-sky OI 630.0 nm airglow imaging, in-situ electron density measurements from low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, together with interplanetary and geomagnetic parameters.

By explicitly linking variations in the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field to storm-time electrodynamic disturbances in the equatorial and low-latitude ionosphere, we identify possible physical conditions under which interplanetary forcing and the ionospheric background state become favorably aligned, enabling the development of SPBs and their preferred longitudinal occurrence over the American sector.

The results reveal, for the events analyzed, a systematic preference for SPB development over low-declination regions of the western American sector, while their occurrence is strongly suppressed over high-declination regions such as northeastern Brazil, even under comparable geomagnetic forcing, within a consistent seasonal background.

This recurrent pattern indicates that storm-time SPB occurrence is constrained by declination-controlled electrodynamics, particularly through the alignment of the solar terminator with the magnetic meridian and the associated modulation of flux-tube-integrated Pedersen conductance.

These results provide observational constraints on the coupling between interplanetary drivers and ionospheric electrodynamics controlling the development and localization of SPBs and support the improvement of storm-time ionospheric modeling and forecasting over the American sector.

title: Global Ionospheric Disturbances Induced by Solar Flares During the Main and Recovery Phases of the May 2024 Superstorm Under High Solar Activity

sentences.text: Between 10 and 17 May 2024, the solar active region AR3664 produced the most intense coronal mass ejection (CME) recorded in the past two decades, leading to geomagnetic superstorm.
During this geomagnetic superstorm, two solar flares (SFs) occurred under distinct geomagnetic conditions.
The first flare took place during the main phase of the storm (SYM-H = ─518 nT; Kp = 9), while the second occurred in the end of the recovery phase (SYM-H = ─53 nT; Kp = 2─).

In this study, ground-based magnetometer observations, together with GPS-derived vertical total electron content (VTEC) and rate of TEC (ROT) data, are used to examine the spatial and temporal electrodynamics of the ionosphere across a broad geographic region.
The analysis focuses on the ionospheric response to both solar flares, emphasizing their occurrence during different geomagnetic storm phases.
From a space weather perspective, this work provides new insights into the coupled effects of geomagnetic disturbances and Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances (SIDs) induced by solar flares.
Furthermore, variations in the equatorial electrojet (EEJ) are investigated to elucidate the electrodynamic processes operating during these extreme solar─terrestrial events.

title: Equatorial Ionospheric Response to the May 11, 2024, Geomagnetic Superstorm over Ecuador

sentences.text: This study examines how an extreme G5 geomagnetic storm affected the ionosphere over Ecuador, including the Galápagos Islands, from 10 to 13 May 2024.

We used data from multiple GPS stations to measure the Total Electron Content (TEC), which represents the number of electrons in the ionosphere and directly affects satellite communication and navigation signals.
We also monitored the horizontal component of the magnetic field, which is highly sensitive to geomagnetic disturbances.

During the storm's peak (10─11 May), the TEC decreased by about 30 TEC units, while the horizontal magnetic field dropped by more than 400 nT. This decrease in TEC, instead of the typical increase seen in some storms, was caused by storm-driven changes in the upper atmosphere that accelerated electron loss and disrupted normal ionospheric processes.
These results show that severe geomagnetic storms can strongly affect the equatorial ionosphere and emphasize the need for continuous monitoring to protect satellite-based systems.

title: Longitudinal variation of ionospheric irregularities and response of the ionosphere during May and October 2024 geomagnetic storms

abbreviations.RODI: rate of change of electron density Ne index
abbreviations.ROTI: rate of change of TEC index

sentences.text: We examine the response of the ionosphere to the May and October 2024 geomagnetic storms, the two recent great geomagnetic storms of solar cycle 25.
We identified the occurrence of ionospheric irregularities during the two geomagnetic storms.

We used percentage change in vertical total electron content (∆VTEC%) computed using VTEC data from three equatorial ground-based global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receivers in the American, African, and Asian sectors, to study the ionospheric response.

In order to determine the occurrence of ionospheric irregularities, we employed the rate of change of electron density (Ne) index (RODI) from Swarm satellite-A (Sw-A) and the rate of change of TEC index (ROTI) from the GNSS TEC.
We found that the longitudinal response to the two storms were different in terms of TEC and irregularities as a function of storm phase.
Our results revealed a positive ionospheric storm over the African and Asian sectors during the main phase of May storm; whereas a negative ionospheric response was recorded over the American sector.
In contrast, during the October storm, a positive ionospheric storm effect was observed over the American and African sectors and negatively over the Asian sector.

Additionally, we identified that the October storm had a higher percentage irregularity occurrence rate than the May storm, although the May storm's G5 level was higher than the October storm's G4 level.
All sectors experienced irregularities during the two main storms phases, with the exception of the American sector during the May 2024 storm, when an inhibition was observed.
Sw-A showed a longitudinal trend in the occurrence rate of irregularities during the May storm, with America having the lowest rate, followed by Africa and Asia.
During the October storm, this longitudinal dependence is reversed, with irregularities occurring over the America, Africa and Asia, respectively, from the highest to lowest.

The findings of this study provide the scientific community with new insights into how geomagnetic storms influence ionospheric plasma structure, occurrence of irregularities, and can help improve space weather prediction and modeling.

title: Prominent Ionospheric Responses Throughout the Multiple Different Altitudes in the Asian-Australian Sector During the May 2024 Mother's Day Storm

abbreviations.SYM-H: symmetric component of the ring current

sentences.text: During strong geomagnetic storms, the ionosphere can be significantly disturbed, impacting communications, navigation, and spacecraft operations.
The ionospheric responses to the geomagnetic storms have become one of the most important research topics, as storms alter electron density distributions.

The May 2024 superstorm is the strongest geomagnetic storm in the past two decades and this study mainly focuses on the prominent ionospheric altitudinal responses in the Asian-Australian sector using data from multiple Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellites.

During the minimum symmetric component of the ring current (SYM-H) period from ∼22:00 UT on 10 May to ∼12:00 UT on 11 May, LEO-based total electron content (TEC) revealed a prolonged and large-scale daytime meridional enhancement, with maximum increases of 250%─450% and extending to above 800 km, likely driven by storm-time neutral winds and disturbed electric fields.
For the topside nighttime enhancement on 11 May in the northern Asian-Australian sector, both enhanced H^+/N_i and vertical drifts suggested that the plasmasphere refilling made major contributions.
LEO-based and ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) TECs exhibited opposite responses in the southern Asian-Australian region.
Two distinct electron density profiles in the Australian and Indonesian regions were depicted, highlighting the differences linked to thermospheric compositions and dynamics/electrodynamics.
These physical processes occurred throughout multiple different altitudes from bottomside to topside ionosphere, showing the severe impact of superstorms.

title: Evolution of Ionospheric Irregularities Over the American Sector During the May 2024 Geomagnetic Superstorm

sentences.text: Ionospheric F-region irregularities are typical post-sunset background electron density inhomogeneous structures that are both storm-induced and naturally occurring equatorial plasma bubble (EPB) phenomena.

Their dynamic morphology and latitudinal occurrence differ depending on the observational technique, including ionograms from ionosondes and ROT and ROTI derived from GPS-TEC measurements, which are commonly used to detect equatorial spread-F (ESF) and EPB-related irregularities.
In this study, we investigate how the May 2024 geomagnetic storm modified ionospheric conditions over the American sector during a 30-day interval spanning quiet and storm-time periods.

Manually scaled ionograms from Araguatins (ARA; within the equatorial anomaly: 5.6°S, 48.1°W, dip latitude 6.2°S) and São José dos Campos (SJC; outside the equatorial anomaly: 23.2°S, 46.0°W, dip latitude 22.1°S) were used to derive h'F, foF2, and ESF occurrence in both range and frequency spread-F.
These results were compared with irregularity structures detected from ROT and ROTI across 14 GPS-TEC stations distributed over eastern and western America.
The analysis reveals strong agreement between the techniques and significant storm-induced enhancements in ESF and F-region irregularities.

The observed structures are attributed to the combined effects of post-sunset pre-reversal enhancement (PRE), dusk-side prompt penetration electric fields (PPEF), and storm-time neutral wind─driven dynamo electric fields.

title: Features of ionospheric irregularities in the transitional low-to-mid latitudes observed from anomaly crest location

sentences.text: Equatorial ionospheric irregularities intersect and interfere with transionospheric radio signals often resulting in serious degradation of their performance including that of satellite-based systems and services.
While such phenomena are associated with geomagnetic disturbed conditions in the mid and high latitudes, they could occur even under geomagnetic quiet conditions in the equatorial and low latitudes.
The radio frequency signals affected also varies across a wide spectrum extending from VHF to L-band and often S-band as well.

Some novel coordinated experimental observations were recorded during February-March 2024 using University of Calcutta VHF radar operating at 53 MHz at the Ionosphere Field Station, Haringhata (22.93N, 88.37E geographic; 35N magnetic dip) and GPS L-band measurements from North Bengal University (NBU) (26.71N, 88.35E geographic; 42N magnetic dip).
The present paper reports three cases which occurred on February 23, March 18 and 28, 2024.

The Radar beam has to be directed towards the north from Haringhata in order to achieve the condition of orthogonality with the magnetic field lines around a subionospheric location of 25N, 88E. On March 18, 2024, the VHF radar backscattered signals noted a number of irregularity patches occurring around 20:30, 22:00 and 23:30 LT respectively at heights ranging from 300-650 km.
The GPS links studied from NBU were limited over a swath of 22-26.5N and 86-91E so as to observe a common ionospheric volume.
On March 18, 2024, TEC depletion was noted on the SV18 link around 24:00 LT while SV29 experienced depletions around 21:00-21:30 LT and SV32 around 23:15-23:30 LT.
Similar analyses have also been for February 23 and March 28, 2024.
These novel coordinated measurements validate the simultaneous coexistence of ionospheric irregularities of varying scale sizes ranging from centimeters to metres using the VHF radar and GPS.
However, an outstanding issue to consider is the occurrence of ionospheric irregularities even at L-band at a magnetic dip of 39N during late evening and midnight hours.
This brings forth the question whether these irregularities could be attributed to equatorial plasma bubbles or to some remnants of transitional mid-latitude plasma density structures.
Further work is underway on these aspects.

title: Comparative GNSS Amplitude Scintillation Characteristics in Brazilian Low Latitudes During Four Intense Magnetic Storms

sentences.text: This work presents the GNSS amplitude scintillation characteristics over Brazilian sites during the magnetic storms of May 2024, October 2024, November 2025 and January 2026.
The scintillation characteristics for São José dos Campos are: on May 2024 (max Dst -406 nT) a super bubble moving to the west triggered scintillation with S4 up to 0.7 on the night 10/11.
May (winter solstice) is a month when scintillations are not expected over Brazil, since the period of scintillation extends from about September to April.
Many publications have already been published about this extremely strong storm.
In October 2024, scintillation inhibition was observed on the nights 07/08 (max Dst -148 nT) and 10/11 (max Dst -333 nT).
In November 2025, 11/12 (max Dst -209 nT) strong scintillation was triggered with S4>1.2 and in January 2026, during the night 20 (max Dst -218 nT), scintillation was inhibited.
Even though the maximum Dst intensities and their times of occurrence were almost the same for November 2025 and January 2026 events, very different scintillation characteristics were observed.
Ionosonde data will be used to infer the ionospheric characteristics during these storms.
S4 regional maps during these storms will be provided.
The latitudinal differences in the scintillation behavior and discussions about the physical mechanisms responsible for the observed storm-time characteristics will be presented.

title: GNSS TEC Observation of Storm Enhanced Density, Polar Ionospheric Tongue of Ionization and Polar Ionization Hole During the May 10, 2024 Superstorm

sentences.text: This study investigates the simultaneous evolution of storm-enhanced density (SED), the tongue of ionization (TOI), and the polar ionospheric holes (PIH) during the May 10, 2024 geomagnetic superstorm.
Using global GNSS TEC data, differential TEC, and thermospheric O/N₂ measurements from TIMED/GUVI, we analyze plasma and neutral dynamics and their interaction at polar and subauroral latitudes.
Prompt penetration electric fields (PPEF) and SAPS-induced sunward drifts drove the development of a strong SED plume, which was subsequently entrained into the polar cap.
The TOI primarily convected anti-sunward through the throat region, then with a notable eastward component within the polar cap.

Successively, a PIH formed and convected eastward as the neutral gas with a depleted O/N₂ ratio was likely circulating eastward from the morning to afternoon sector under intense ion drag at high latitudes.
The TOI evolved into a large plasma patch due to the influence of the PIH and the accompanying O/N₂-depleted neutral air.
Thus observations suggest that the suppressed O/N₂ region may facilitate the fragmentation of the TOI into distinct patches.
This event underscores the significance of plasma-neutral coupling in shaping the TOI and plasma patches during extreme geomagnetic storms.

title: Unusually strong equatorial ionization anomaly across three local time sectors during the intense 10─11 May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: The Earth's upper atmosphere is significantly influenced by space weather events, particularly geomagnetic storms.
In this study, we investigate the impact of an intense geomagnetic storm that occurred on 10─11 May 2024 on the equatorial and low-latitude ionosphere.
Using datasets from various ground and satellite-based (SWARM and GOLD satellites, Global GNSS receivers, Incoherent Scatter Radar, Fabry-
Perot interferometers, and magnetometers) measurements, we show the impact of extreme prompt penetration of the electric field on the development of the plasma fountain during the storm.
Prompt penetration electric field caused a significant enhancement in the ionospheric vertical drift (∼95 m/s) and the equatorial electrojet strength (∼275 nT) over Jicamarca.
These extreme eastward electric field perturbations, along with the large meridional wind, significantly altered the F-region plasma fountain at different local times.
The afternoon equatorial ionization anomaly (EIA) not only sustained for an exceptionally long duration (∼12 hr) but also expanded spatially over time.
EIA crests extended beyond ±35° MLat in both hemispheres over the Jicamarca meridian during the afternoon and evening hours, eventually merging with the aurora.

This study shows, for the first time, that unusually strong EIA can not only develop at different local times but can also sustain for long durations under favorable conditions, which has implications for space weather applications.

title: Thermospheric Nitric Oxide Variability During a Compound Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: We present an analysis of thermospheric nitric oxide (NO) variability during a compound geomagnetic storm from 1─11 September 2002, consisting of a CIR-driven storm beginning on 4 September followed by an ICME-driven storm on 7 September during the recovery phase of the first (minimum SYM-H = −168 nT).

Geomagnetic storms enhance high-latitude energy deposition, increasing NO production, which acts as a key thermospheric "thermostat" by radiatively cooling the upper atmosphere and modulating neutral density with impacts on satellite orbital drag.
Significant emphasis has been directed toward the impacts of the sudden storm thermospheric heating and our ability (or inability) to nowcast/forecast it correctly.
The ability (or inability) to nowcast/forecast the cooling processes of the thermosphere are equally important for tracking space objects, avoiding collisions, or controlling reentry.

Using NO SABER measurements aboard TIMED (100─160 km; Southern Hemisphere coverage), solar wind observations from Wind, and geomagnetic indices, we construct interpolated NO maps in geographic, centered dipole, and quasi-dipole coordinates to examine local time and latitude variability.

We observe persistent high-latitude diurnal fluctuations independent of coordinate system, storm-time enhancements superposed on this background, and a pronounced asymmetry between midnight and subsolar sectors.

During the ICME phase, strong mid-latitude dayside enhancements emerge hours after nightside intensification, with substantial local time offsets that cannot be explained by simultaneous high-latitude forcing.
TIE-GCM simulations driven by observed solar wind inputs reproduce the amplitude and timing of the ICME-related enhancements, showing strong model-data agreement.

Ongoing work examines full local time model output to determine whether NO co-rotation and thermospheric winds can account for delayed dayside signatures; if transport is insufficient, alternative local generation processes or IMF-dependent cusp dynamics may be required.

These results improve understanding of storm-time thermospheric heating and cooling pathways and their local time dependence, with implications for neutral density specification and satellite drag prediction during compound geomagnetic disturbances.

title: The impact of solar wind high-speed streams and coronal mass ejections on Joule heating and neutral density in low Earth orbit

sentences.text: The near-Earth space environment is strongly influenced by the solar wind and embedded interplanetary magnetic field.

Therefore a thorough understanding of the upper atmosphere response during the passage of geoeffective solar wind transients, such as high-speed streams/stream interaction regions (HSS/SIR) and interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs) is crucial for accurate space weather predictions.

A key mechanism in dissipating the solar wind energy in the upper atmosphere is auroral Joule heating, which causes thermal expansion of the thermosphere, increasing the thermospheric density and causing low Earth orbiting satellites to experience more drag.

Understanding the satellite drag changes related to the increased density during geomagnetic storms is essential for satellite operators to be able to perform the necessary collision avoidance maneuvers.

In this work we characterize the Joule heating in the northern hemisphere and the orbit-averaged neutral density enhancements during storms driven by HSS/SIR, as well as sheath regions and magnetic clouds associated with ICMEs.

Applying a robust method for determining the Joule heating using AMPERE, SuperMAG and SuperDARN data, we study the northern hemispheric Joule heating and global thermospheric neutral density enhancements at Swarm and GRACE satellites during 278 geomagnetic storms between 2010 and 2024 by using superposed epoch analysis.

It is found that the Joule heating in the ionospheric E-region and thermospheric neutral density enhancements at the altitude of the Swarm and GRACE satellites (350 ─ 550 km) show characteristics which depend on the geomagnetic storm driver.
The Joule heating has a fast increase at the beginning of the storm main phase when the storm is initiated by a HSS/SIR or by the sheath region of ICMEs.
In comparison, a more gradual and longer lasting increase is found in storms driven by magnetic clouds within ICMEs.
In all storms Joule heating during the main phase is concentrated on the morning and afternoon auroral oval.

Superposed epoch analysis of the orbit-averaged thermospheric neutral density altitude-adjusted to 450 km shows a gradual increase during the storm main phase, reflecting the time-integrated history of recent Joule heating.
The largest density enhancements occur during magnetic cloud driven storms with a median peak 130% above quiet-time levels.
HSS/SIR-driven storms have the longest-lasting neutral density enhancements, leading to a cumulative effect similar to that of magnetic cloud-driven storms, albeit with a lower peak density (116%).
Sheath storms cause the fastest density increases but have the shortest main phases, resulting in a lower cumulative effect than HSS/SIR or magnetic cloud storms.
The density recovery half-life in the storm recovery phase is 15.3 hours for HSS/SIR storms, significantly longer than for magnetic cloud (9.4 hours) and sheath (7.7 hours) storms.

title: The statistical analysis of the extreme geomagnetically induced currents in power lines in the north-west of Russia

sentences.text: In this work a statistical study of extreme values of geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) in power lines on the North of Russia since 2012 year was conducted.

The Polar Geophysical Institute and the Northern Energy Research Center of the Kola Science Center RAS have created and have been operating the only one GIC recording system in Russia on the "Northern Transit" power transmission line across the Murmansk region and Karelia.

This registration system measures a quasi-DC current in dead-grounded neutral of the transformers at 4 sub-stations: Vykhodnoy (VKH), Titan (TTN), Louhi (LKH), and Kondopoga (KND) on the 330 kV line, and at sub-station Revda (RVD) on the 220 kV line.
For the VKH sub-station CGM Lat=65.5°, for the KND CGM Lat=60.8°.

The extreme values of the GIC for 11 years of observations (2012-2022 years) were analyzed based on data from the auroral substation VKH (92 cases, GIC> 20 A) and the subauroral substation KND (32 cases, GIC> 5 A).
The number of extreme GIC events is higher during the decline and maximum of the solar cycle.
According to the VKH station, GICs reach extreme values more often during CME magnetic storms ( 54.7%) than during CIR magnetic storms (33.7%).
At the same time, 10.5% of GIC cases were observed during substorm without a magnetic storm, 1 % during SC.
According to the KND station, extreme values of GIC are observed during CME storms in 80% of cases.
So CIR magnetic storms, despite their lower intensity, must also be taken into account when forecasting the impact of space weather on technological systems.
Analyses showed that extreme values of GIC are mainly caused by substorms (>80% of cases) in both the post-midnight and pre-midnight MLT sectors.
Daytime jumps of GIC are associated with positive magnetic bays, Pc5 pulsations, SC impulse.
For CME storms, extreme GICs are mainly observed during the main phase of the magnetic storm.
On average, upon an increase of |dB/dt|, a higher GIC magnitude is recorded.
A strong enhancement of GIC coincides with the period of elevated dB/dt.
However, there is no one-to-one correspondence between the GIC and dB/dt magnitudes.
On average, with an increase of the intensity of magnetic storm (SYM-H), substorm (IE), higher GIC values are registered.

But there is no clear linear dependence of the GIC amplitude on the parameters of the interplanetary medium (V, Es, ∊) and geomagnetic indices (IE, AE, SYM-H), which indicates the difficulty of predicting GICs based only on these parameters.
This is because GICs depend on local ionosphere factors: configuration of the ionospheric current systems, frequency of the signal.
To predict the amplitude of the GICs in power lines at high latitudes, we need to know more information about the formation of mesoscale and small-scale ionospheric current systems.
At subauroral latitudes the dB/dt variations show much better correlation with these parameters than GICs.
The study was supported by grant No. 25-17-20038 from the Russian Science Foundation and a grant from the Ministry of Education and Science of the Murmansk Region.

title: Coupled Thermosphere-Ionosphere Dynamics Driven by Geomagnetic Forcing: Observational and Modeling Perspectives

abbreviations.GOLD: Global-Scale Observations of the Limb and Disk

sentences.text: The thermosphere-ionosphere (T-I) system responds in a complex and coupled manner to geomagnetic activity through the transfer of energy and momentum from the magnetosphere to the upper atmosphere.

This study examines the dynamical and electrodynamical responses of the T-I system to varying levels of geomagnetic forcing using a combination of multi-instrument observations and numerical modeling.

Ground-based GNSS-derived total electron content (TEC) and the O/N_2 ratio from the Global-Scale Observations of the Limb and Disk (GOLD) mission are analyzed together with simulations from the Thermosphere-Ionosphere-Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIE-GCM).
The results show pronounced midlatitude enhancements in electron density and thermospheric temperature during geomagnetic storms, accompanied by changes in neutral winds and composition.
Notably, ionospheric irregularities are also observed during geomagnetically quiet periods.
Comparisons between observations and model simulations reveal both the strengths and limitations of the TIE-GCM in reproducing localized ionospheric enhancements.
These findings advance our understanding of geomagnetic forcing in thermosphere-ionosphere coupling and its implications for space weather in the upper atmosphere.

title: Study of an extreme space weather event in South America based on ionospheric indices

sentences.text: There are many kinds of ionospheric indices proposed to show important information about the state of the ionosphere.
Some of them are based on dual frequency GNSS carrier phase measurements.

We utilized GNSS observations from March 17-18, 2015, specifically around the time of the St. Patrick's Day geomagnetic storm and studied the behavior of the following indices: the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI), the Sudden Ionospheric Disturbance Index (SIDX), the Weather Index (W), the Disturbance Ionosphere Index (DIX) and the Ionospheric Gradient Index (GIX) during this extreme Space Weather event.
To assess the sensitivity of the indices to the different phases of the storm, the temporal behaviour of each index was analysed at different magnetic latitudes.
For the calculation of the ROTI, SIDX and DIX indices, the geometry-free combination method was used instead of VTEC values, employing all available GNSS constellations and frequency combinations.
Based on our study, we can affirm that local time and geomagnetic latitude significantly influence the ionospheric indices.
This result is related to the evolution of electrodynamic processes during the development of the magnetic storm.
A relevant outcome is the response of the indices in the different phases of the storm in the mid-latitude region.

We observe that during the positive phase of the storm, the space-time gradient increases as a result of the greater contribution of electric fields, thermospheric winds and other factors, which accelerates the increase in VTEC.
Meanwhile, during the negative phase, the overall effect of these processes on the ionosphere decreases, slowing down the growth of VTEC and, in some cases, even causing a decrease.

title: Monitoring Storm-Time Low-Latitude Ionospheric Disturbances over India Using NavIC/IRNSS

sentences.text: This study investigates low-latitude ionospheric responses over the Indian region during six intense geomagnetic storms between 2017 and 2024, including the extreme May 2024 superstorm, using NavIC/IRNSS and IGS observations.
Variations in Total Electron Content (TEC), Rate of TEC Index (ROTI), and scintillation index (S4) are analysed using data from a NavIC receiver at Sangli (16.5°N, 74.3°E) and regional GNSS stations.

The observed responses are examined in relation to interplanetary conditions, geomagnetic indices, Equatorial Electrojet (EEJ) variability, storm-time electric fields, and thermospheric composition changes (O/N₂).
CME-driven storms produced rapid daytime TEC enhancements, whereas CIR─HSS storms caused prolonged disturbances.

The May 2024 superstorm (Dst ≍ −412 nT) resulted in widespread TEC depletion with brief flare-induced enhancements, demonstrating the effectiveness of NavIC/IRNSS for monitoring storm-time ionospheric variability.

title: Ionosphere Responses during Geomagnetic Storm and Quiet Events via GNSS CM01 Receiver in Thailand

sentences.text: Ionospheric variability is a critical component of space weather, particularly in low-latitude regions near the geomagnetic equator, where ionospheric dynamics are strongly influenced by geomagnetic activity.

This study investigates ionospheric responses over Thailand during geomagnetic storm and quiet conditions in November 2025, using Total Electron Content (TEC) derived from the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) CM01 receiver.
The CM01 station is located at 98^∘57^'18.9^'' E and 18^∘48^'07.94^'' N, at an altitude of 305.8 m in northern Thailand.
This near-geomagnetic-equator location makes the site well suited for examining storm-time ionospheric disturbances and equatorial plasma processes.
