title: Solar energetic He access into the Van Allen radiation belts: SEP event of September 2017

sentences.text: We investigate the penetration solar He ions into the outer Van Allen belt during large SEP events during the September of 2017.
Very high solar activity, resulted in four X-class flares and 27 M-class flares between September 6─10, resulting in major SEP events including GLE activity.
We use the REPT (relativistic Electron Proton Telescope) data onboard the Van Allen Probes mission to characterize the penetration of solar energetic Helium into the outer Van Allen belt.

While REPT mainly measures energetic electrons and protons, it also records pulse height analyzed data (PHA) of each individual particle measured for a set of hundred particles at approximately 12 ms cadence.
SEP-He are identified using these PHA data.
We measure He spectra and their temporal evolution during the course of the event period.
We note that from a space weather perspective, He ions deposit energy through rapid ionization resulting in single event upsets (SEU) whereas protons do that via nuclear interactions.

title: Sun radio interferometer space experiment (SunRISE): mission updates and launch planning

sentences.text: NASA's Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment (SunRISE), slated to launch in the summer of 2026, will reveal aspects of how solar energetic particles (SEPs) are accelerated at coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and how SEPs are released into interplanetary space.

SunRISE is composed of a constellation of six identical small spacecraft of a 6U CubeSat form factor, mounted with radio antenna paired with global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receivers that will form the first low radio frequency (0.1 MHz to 25 MHz) space-based radio interferometer capable of resolved radio observations to locate and track decametric-hectometric (DH) radio bursts as they expand out into the corona.
Studying the emission from these bursts will reveal valuable insight into particle acceleration associated with CMEs (Type II bursts) and solar flares (Type III bursts).

In addition, tracking the emission as the particles are accelerated through the inner heliosphere will reveal the magnetic topology of solar wind structures and give insight into regions with enhanced particle acceleration.
The six spacecraft that form the SunRISE interferometer will fly in passive formation, with a nominal baseline of 10 km, in a supersynchronous geosynchronous Earth orbit (super-GEO).
Flying above the ionosphere, SunRISE will provide continuous observations of part of the radio spectra tuned to track particle acceleration and transport between 0.2 R_⊙ to 20 R_⊙.
A combination of on-board processing and ground processing will provide high resolution position determination for localizing radio emission.
At the time of the COSPAR Scientific Assembly, SunRISE will be planning for imminent launch.
We describe the technical nature of the mission, the science processing required to track DH Type II and III bursts, as well as updates on the mission.
While SunRISE is a mission conducting science in its own right, it also is intended to be a pathfinder for future missions.
We provide an initial assessment of the "experience gained" for future mission, from the perspective of both the SunRISE science and technical implementation.
Part of this research was carried out at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, under a contract with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

title: Storm-Time Thermospheric Density Enhancements During Solar Cycle 25: Multi-Level Orbitography and Implications for Space Debris Dynamics

sentences.text: The ascending and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25 have been marked by a sequence of intense solar flares and fast coronal mass ejections (CMEs), producing several major geomagnetic storms and significant perturbations of the near-Earth space environment.

Among the most impactful events are the geomagnetic storms of February 3─4, 2022 (associated with the loss of multiple Starlink satellites), April 23─24, 2023, the severe storm of May 10─11, 2024—one of the strongest of the current cycle—and additional extreme disturbances observed in March and October 2025 near solar maximum.
These events led to substantial thermospheric heating and rapid density enhancements in low Earth orbit (LEO), dramatically increasing atmospheric drag and altering satellite and debris trajectories.

This contribution aims to establish a quantitative bridge between major solar events and thermospheric total density variations, as revealed by satellite orbitography, with a particular emphasis on implications for space debris dynamics.
The study is based on two complementary orbitographic approaches.
The first approach relies on precise orbit determination of laser-ranged geodetic satellites, including Starlette ( 800 km altitude), Stella ( 800 km), Ajisai ( 1490 km), and LARES ( 1450 km).
Their orbits are reconstructed over short arcs using Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) data accumulated by the global network of the International Laser Ranging Service (ILRS).
The combined measurements from multiple stations worldwide allow centimeter-level orbit reconstruction with high temporal resolution.

During geomagnetic storms, short-arc solutions make it possible to identify rapid variations in non-gravitational accelerations and to retrieve equivalent thermospheric density changes with near-minute resolution.
This deterministic framework provides a highly sensitive reference for characterizing storm-time drag at specific altitudes relevant to debris populations.
The second approach exploits extended time series of Two-Line Element (TLE) data.

Although limited to kilometer-level accuracy, TLE datasets offer two key advantages: they enable individual trajectory analyses of objects with sufficiently high area-to-mass ratios, revealing storm-time semi-major axis decay, and they allow statistical investigations over large populations of operational satellites and debris fragments in LEO and MEO.
Long-term orbital adjustments and propagations are performed to characterize the cumulative impact of geomagnetic storms on orbital energy loss and lifetime reduction.
The objectives of the study are threefold.
First, we identify major solar and geomagnetic events from 2022 to 2025 that significantly modified thermospheric density at satellite altitudes.
Second, we quantify the corresponding orbital signatures using both centimeter-level SLR orbitography or long-term TLE-based analyses.

Third, we investigate the physical drivers of the observed drag enhancement, focusing on (i) the satellite's local solar time (LST), which modulates thermospheric response through day─night asymmetries, and (ii) selected solar proxies used as inputs to thermospheric density models (e.g., F10.7 flux and geomagnetic indices).
From a space debris perspective, storm-time density enhancements can temporarily accelerate orbital decay, modify conjunction statistics, and significantly alter predicted re-entry timelines.
While increased drag may contribute to debris mitigation at certain altitudes, it also introduces short-term uncertainties in orbit prediction and collision risk assessment.

The comparison between high-precision SLR-based density retrievals and large-scale TLE statistical behavior provides insight into the reliability of current thermospheric models for debris environment forecasting during extreme space-weather conditions.

Preliminary results indicate that severe geomagnetic storms produce rapid density increases clearly detectable in centimeter-level orbit reconstructions, while TLE-based analyses reveal broader population-level trends.

The amplitude of drag enhancement appears strongly dependent on local solar time, suggesting that global geomagnetic indices alone cannot capture the full spatio-temporal variability of storm-time density response.

These findings underline the necessity of improved storm-time thermospheric modeling for robust debris propagation, operational orbit determination, and long-term sustainability of the near-Earth space environment during periods of intense solar activity.

title: Altitude-dependent tracking degradation during the 19th January 2026 geomagnetic storm: implications for Starlink's orbital lowering strategy

sentences.text: Space activity is accelerating rapidly, with almost 15,000 active satellites currently in Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
As launch rates continue to rise, accurately tracking objects in space is critical for collision avoidance and space safety.
Two-Line Element (TLE) sets, orbital element data made publicly available by the US Space Command, are updated by tracking systems and use SGP4 to model satellite trajectories.
A significant drop in TLE update frequency indicates tracking degradation ─
a reduced ability to locate objects, and in severe cases a complete loss of tracking.

This becomes particularly challenging during geomagnetic storms, where interaction between solar activity, Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere causes quick, unpredictable changes that perturb satellite trajectories and compromise tracking ability.
Atmospheric drag also increases dramatically within hours, yet predictive models struggle to capture this variability.
This means we become more reliant on frequent tracking updates precisely when tracking systems are least able to provide them.

Between 19 ─ 24 January 2026, an X1.9 solar flare followed by a coronal mass ejection (CME) produced the strongest (S4) solar radiation storm since the 2003 Halloween storm, with proton flux levels exceeding 104 Protons/(cm^2 s sr) for particles above 10 MeV and a Kp index over 8.
Coinciding with this, SpaceX initiated a large-scale altitude migration of over 4,000 Starlink satellites, from approximately 550km to 480km for the purpose of space safety.
This convergence of a major space weather and major operational event makes this period a relevant case study.
This study investigates the impact of this storm on tracking ability for all active LEO satellites across January 2026, separated into 7 altitude bands ranging from 300 - 2000km.

Per band, we examine metrics including TLE update frequency (TLEs per satellite per day), semi-major axis evolution, and orbital decay rate across three time periods (before, during and after the storm).
This enables quantifying altitude-dependent tracking degradation across LEO.
For the Starlink constellation specifically, we assess evidence of the orbit lowering manoeuvres and whether the storm accelerated, decelerated or disrupted the migration.

We also examine how lower altitudes affects station-keeping propellant requirements, manoeuvre budget, and satellite lifetime, providing insight into the long-term operational consequences of this migration strategy.
As we transition out of a solar maximum, characterising how geomagnetic storms affect tracking across altitudes is essential for understanding satellite responses to storm-driven perturbations.

With mega-constellations growing in scale and undergoing large operational changes, this work will draw conclusions that inform future strategies for commercial satellite management, with direct implications for collision avoidance and long-term space safety.

title: JW-FVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Closed-Loop Solar Flare Forecasting

sentences.text: As the most violent eruptive phenomena in the solar system, solar flares constitute a critical source of hazardous space weather, capable of inflicting severe disruptions on satellite constellations and terrestrial power grids.

Yet, to date, research has focused primarily on improving forecast accuracy within a passive paradigm, failing to translate predictive insights into the autonomous driving of observational instruments.
Consequently, telescope operations rely heavily on manual intervention based on human experience.
This reliance prevents the timely activation of high-cadence 'flare modes', resulting in the inevitable loss of critical data during the rapid onset of impulsive eruptions.
To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework, pioneering the application of embodied intelligence in space weather monitoring.
Unlike traditional classifiers, our model integrates the semantic reasoning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to synchronously process solar active region magnetograms and textual physical parameters.
Crucially, it functions as an end-to-end agent, directly outputting executable commands to drive ground-based telescopes, thereby bypassing the bottleneck of manual interpretation.

Preliminary validation on dataset demonstrates that the system achieves state-of-the-art performance in identifying major X-class flares, maintaining high True Skill Statistics (TSS) while enabling autonomous telescope control.

By autonomously switching instruments to flare mode based on predictive priors, this work establishes the first closed-loop VLA system, significantly enhancing the capture of eruptive dynamics and paving the way for next-generation intelligent observatories.

title: Advancing Ionospheric Mapping and Forecasting through Probabilistic Deep Learning

sentences.text: The ionosphere represents the ionized region of Earth's upper atmosphere, acting as a highly dynamic interface between our planet and the near-Earth space environment.
Its variability, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic disturbances, poses significant challenges for global navigation and satellite communication.
Accurate characterization of the Total Electron Content (TEC) is essential for supporting space weather monitoring and mitigating navigation errors.
However, traditional models often struggle to capture small-scale variations or provide reliable confidence metrics during extreme space weather events.
This presentation provides an overview of our recent progress in developing deep learning (DL) frameworks designed to enhance ionospheric monitoring and prediction.
Central to our work is the integration of Uncertainty Quantification (UQ).

By employing deep ensembles, Bayesian layers, and transformer-based architectures, our models generate high-resolution global products that provide both precise TEC estimates and their associated predictive uncertainties.

We demonstrate that these uncertainty metrics are not merely diagnostic but provide useful information when correcting single-frequency GNSS observations for ionospheric effects, leading to reduced positioning errors.
Furthermore, we discuss the integration of multi-source data, including GNSS, satellite altimetry, and radio occultation, to mitigate spatial data sparsity, particularly over oceanic regions.
Beyond vertical TEC mapping, we introduce direct slant modeling, which eliminates the need for assumptions regarding electron density distribution ─
a common limitation in traditional approaches.

Overall, these developments demonstrate that deep learning is an exceptionally powerful and versatile tool for improving the quality and reliability of ionospheric products in space weather and navigation applications.

title: How to deal with space environment models to compute induced effects, using OMERE and FASTRAD®

sentences.text: Since decades, a wide range of models have been developed to compute the trapped particles, solar flares and Galactic Cosmic Rays fluxes for a dedicated mission.

OMERE freeware, downloaded by a large amount of people all around the world, was designed to use these models and compute the induced effects such as Single Event Effects (SEE) or solar cell degradation.
FASTRAD® software was also developed to compute, among other things, the Total Ionizing Dose (TID) at component level, considering a 3D realistic geometry of different units and components.

We will present the basic process to deal with these programs in order to first define, in an easy way, the space environment of some dedicated missions (LEO, EOR, GEO, …) with the corresponding models (IRENE, AE8/AP8, GCR ISO 15390, …).
Then, we will present SEE rates, solar cell degradation and TID level calculations using realistic components and 3D geometries.
It will allow us to illustrate the impact of space environment models on the induced effects.

title: Radiation Monitors for Space weather onboard Japan Meteorological satellite "Himawari 10" in GEO

sentences.text: Continuous monitoring of energetic electrons and protons across a broad energy range has not yet been established in geostationary orbit over Japan.
This lack of sustained observations remains one of the major obstacles to accurately evaluating radiation‑induced anomalies in spacecraft.

To continuously monitors the space environment and establish accurate assessment of the radiation-induced anomalies, the Radiation Monitors for Space weather (RMS) will be installed on the upcoming geostationary meteorological satellite, Himawari 10.
RMS provides decade-long measurements of the radiation environment at the geostationary orbit over Japan.
RMS consists of two energetic‑electron monitors (RMS‑e1 and RMS-e2), one energetic‑proton monitor (RMS‑p), and a dedicated data‑processing unit (RMS‑dpu).
RMS‑e1 and RMS‑e2, mounted on the north‑ and west‑facing panels of Himawari‑10, measure electrons from 50 keV to 6 MeV.

These observations provide critical information for understanding energetic‑electron environments responsible for deep and internal charging, a major driver of discharge‑related anomalies inside spacecraft.
RMS‑p, installed on the west‑facing panel, measures protons from 10 MeV to 1 GeV.
These measurements enable observations for solar energetic particles (SEPs) associated with solar flares and galactic cosmic rays (GCRs).
Such energetic protons can induce single‑event effects (SEEs), including SEU, SET, and SEL, which may lead to critical failures in spacecraft systems.
Himawari‑10 will downlink one‑second electron and proton spectra to ground stations, and the data will be immediately transferred to NICT facilities via the ground network.
RMS also generates list‑mode data for individual particle events.
Because event rates can occasionally exceed the available telemetry bandwidth, the RMS‑dpu incorporates 2 GB of flash memory to buffer data and prevent loss during temporary burst periods.
The RMS dataset will support not only space‑weather operational services but also scientific studies of radiation‑belt electron dynamics and SEP and GCR phenomena.
Himawari‑10 is scheduled for launch in 2030, with in‑orbit observations planned through 2040.
Initial on‑orbit calibration will be performed through comparison with measurements from Arase and GOES.

title: Deriving SEP Proton Fluxes with the JUICE Radiation Environment Monitor: Response-Matrix Inversion and Near-Conjunction Validation with IREM

sentences.text: Radiation environments driven by solar energetic particle (SEP) events are a key risk for deep-space missions, and robust flux retrievals are essential for both operations and long-term environment models.
We present an end-to-end proton flux inversion pipeline for the Radiation-Hard Electron Monitor (RADEM) on ESA's JUICE mission, focusing on the proton detector channels in the nominal configuration.

We apply a normalization that converts Geant4 simulation counts into calibrated response-matrix elements, consistent with the General Particle Source (GPS) setup (surface source on a sphere) and a cosine-weighted angular distribution within a finite cone.
The response matrix is then used with multiple inversion approaches and time-averaging schemes to retrieve proton intensities in predefined energy bands.
To validate absolute scaling and spectral behavior, we compare RADEM-derived proton time series for selected SEP events with contemporaneous IREM (INTEGRAL Radiation Environment Monitor)
Level-2 proton differential fluxes integrated over matching energy bands.
The comparison includes quiet-time intervals before and after each event and focuses on periods when JUICE and IREM were in close spatial proximity.
We discuss practical sensitivities across the tested inversion approaches and outline how these analyses can support broader heliospheric energetic particle studies across missions.
We will also assess the implications of the first years of RADEM measurements around solar maximum for radiation levels of future space missions between Venus and Mars heliocentric distance.

title: Aviation Radiation Mitigation Strategy Validation

sentences.text: The validation of a strategy for aviation radiation hazard mitigation in development for decades has been completed using two commercial airline flights in 2024 and 2025.

This article provides a historical review of the primary elements leading to that strategy, including the emergence of aviation radiation awareness and collaborative efforts by global aviation and radiological bodies that established mitigation standards.
The primary radiation sources, galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) and solar energetic particles (SEPs), and their mechanisms of impact on Earth's atmosphere are summarized.
The article highlights the biological effects of radiation exposure influenced by altitude, latitude, and geomagnetic conditions, upon aircrew, frequent flyers, and commercial space travelers.
It recognizes a recent SWAG user needs survey report that identifies the need for continuous monitoring and predictive models to ensure long-term occupational and public health safety.
With this backdrop the validation of an ALARA-based strategy was accomplished using two UAL 990 flights on B777-200 aircraft between San Francisco and Paris.
Each carried the same ARMAS FM7 radiation monitoring unit, where one flight occurred during the extreme geomagnetic storm (Gannon storm)
May 10─11, 2024 and one flight occurred during quiet geomagnetic conditions June 8─9, 2025.
The flights' results validated the strategy during extreme space weather, i.e., by applying operational controls for shielding to reduce dose.
One approach is flying lower magnetic latitudes to gain more Earth magnetic field shielding and the other is flying lower altitudes to use atmosphere depth shielding.
Both ALARA shielding methods are controllable in airline operations and air traffic management.
These have now been validated with total dose measurements by ARMAS.
This study shows the effectiveness of the strategy to deviate flight paths to lower magnetic latitude routes and lower altitudes during major geomagnetic storms.
Not only does this approach mitigate HF communication outages but it also reduces risks from increased GNSS errors for take-off and landing navigation.
Magnetic field shielding is a major risk reduction factor for radiation, communication, and navigation while altitude shielding reduces radiation hazard risks.

title: A comprehensive analysis of the May 2024 'great' geomagnetic storm: from solar origin to near-Earth impacts

sentences.text: The great geomagnetic storm of May 10─16, 2024—driven primarily by a series of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from Active Region (AR) 13664—was the most intense geomagnetic event in over two decades, capturing widespread scientific and public attention.
The event was further compounded by a solar energetic particle (SEP) event beginning on May 11, classified as a ground-level enhancement (GLE).
The effects of these space weather events on space assets and humans can be varied and complex, depending on both time and location.
During May 10-16, 2024, the main impacts included the severe geomagnetic storm in geospace and space radiation from SEPs.
Such an intense geomagnetic storm can have numerous potentially harmful effects, including disruptions to power grids, navigation, communication systems, and satellite altitude/attitude control.
It can also increase satellite drag, complicating precise orbit determination and collision avoidance efforts, and cause charging effects on satellite components.
SEPs can lead to single-event effects on space hardware, pose radiation risks to humans in space, and affect avionics and aviation operations.
Summary of actual impacts will be presented.

We employ tools, models, and resources available at the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) to analyze this storm from a system-science perspective, tracing its evolution from solar origin through propagation to its effects on the near-Earth environment, with particular emphasis on inner magnetosphere dynamics.
Finally, we discuss what constitutes a 'great' solar storm from impact perspectives.

title: Lessons-learned from November 2025 and January 2026 events: impacts, gap-analysis and future recommendations

sentences.text: The recent space weather events of late 2025 and early 2026 provided a timely emphasis on the continuous need for global space weather monitoring throughout the descending phase of the solar cycle.
These events can be used as a practical stress test for aviation operations, satellite services, and power grid resilience.
This work presents a case study of the November 2025 and the January 2026 events, comparing their physical drivers, space weather impacts and operational implications.

While both events relate to the arrival of fast Earth-directed coronal mass ejections (CMEs), the events differ in severity of the accompanying solar energetic particle flux levels and induced geomagnetic activity.

The November 2025 event was characterized by a series of high-energy solar proton enhancements associated with major solar flares and fast CMEs, resulting in elevated radiation levels at aviation altitudes, degradation of high-frequency (HF) communications in polar regions, and likely increased single-event upsets in satellite systems.

The recommendations for the airlines operating polar routes in such cases are to consider altitude adjustments and rerouting strategies in accordance with space weather advisories, while for satellite operators this event is expected to trigger mitigation protocols to safeguard sensitive components.
The January 2026 event was driven by the arrival of a fast ICME and the passage of a magnetic structure with an unusually strong interplanetary magnetic field.
This led to close to extreme geomagnetic storms with associated HF COM degradation in the polar regions.

It is expected to have resulted in geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), posing concerns about power grid stability and possible intermittent disruptions to power transmission infrastructure at high latitudes.
Both events have resulted in expected GNSS signal degradation with the event in January having particularly strong impacts on the wide-area augmentation systems widely used by the aviation community.
The events have also brought beautiful auroras down to Europe.
In this study we will present a brief analysis of these two events, showing the related arrival and impact forecasts.
We will present the space weather advisories sent to aviation sector and discuss how they agree with actual impacts.
We will use that comparison to built on future recommendations for the service provision.

title: Space Environment Impacts on Launch and Initial Spacecraft Flight Operations

sentences.text: The space environment can impact launch vehicles and spacecraft during the initial hours of flight.

Flight constraints in the form of space weather launch commit criteria (LCC) where launch operations are delayed if the LCC parameters exceed a prescribed condition are often used as operational controls for space environment risks to protect launch vehicles from extreme space environments during launch operations.
Typically, these constraints are based on real-time measurements of the solar proton flux with a goal of avoiding single event upsets in mission critical avionics.
Space environment flight constraints can also be used to avoid impacts from other space environments including meteor showers, increased drag during geomagnetic storms, and spacecraft charging.

This paper will first discuss the basis of space weather LCCs and what space weather operators and launch industry personnel need to consider when developing meaningful, relevant and actionable LCCs for space weather conditions.

We will then present case studies of launch operations that have been impacted by space weather events including meteoroids and orbital debris, solar particle events, and geomagnetic storms to demonstrate the space weather conditions during and after launch operations of importance to launch operations, the resulting impacts to the mission, and what—if anything—could have been done to better protect the flight hardware from space weather effects.

title: Defence-Oriented Space Weather Services: From Indices to Operational Decisions

sentences.text: Solar Cycle 25 has already delivered a level of activity that few stakeholders expected at its start, including the May 2024 extreme geomagnetic storm, unusually strong flaring, repeated ionospheric disturbances, and atmospheric drag enhancements that affected LEO satellite operations.
These events did not only test models and monitoring chains.
They exposed something more consequential: even when the space environment is well described, decision makers may still lack the information they need to act.
Defence users experience this gap most acutely, operating under tight timelines, high consequence thresholds, and constraints on sharing operational impact data.

In this presentation, we synthesize the main outcomes of our recent assessment of Solar Cycle 25 impacts across satellites, GNSS, HF communications, radiation hazards, and critical infrastructure, with explicit implications for security and defence operations.

We connect these findings to the conclusions of the ESWW 2025 Topical Discussion Meeting "Meeting Defence Needs: Tailoring Space Weather Services for Military Operations," where defence stakeholders and service providers jointly examined what is still missing for operational readiness.
A consistent message emerged: classifications and indices are necessary but not sufficient.

Operational users require precise, impact-oriented statements on onset, duration, geographic footprint, severity, confidence, and expected recovery, expressed in a language aligned with mission risk rather than solar physics.

Using the May 2024 storm as an anchor case, we show how atmospheric expansion altered the risk landscape for LEO constellations, how GNSS degradation becomes operationally meaningful only when mapped to integrity and timing requirements, and why ionospheric intermittency remains a fundamental trust limiter, particularly at high latitudes.

We also examine a recurrent challenge raised in the TDM discussions: short-lived phenomena such as solar radio bursts may not be practically forecastable, yet they can trigger high-cost operational responses, making rapid attribution and post-event confirmation as critical as prediction itself.

We argue that the next step for space weather services is a structural shift from environment-centric reporting toward explicit impact modelling, embedded within robust Research-to-Operations and Operations-to-Research feedback loops.

We outline pragmatic pathways compatible with sensitive operational domains, including minimal incident schemas, anonymized correlation approaches, alignment of forecast products with operational planning cycles, and the continued integration of human expert assessment within real-time workflows.
Solar Cycle 25 has provided an unusually rich operational learning set.
The question we pose is whether we will translate these lessons into trusted, impact-based services before the next extreme event tests our systems again.

title: Swarm gradient products NeGIX and TEGIX for ionospheric perturbation monitoring and modeling studies

sentences.text: Accurate forecasting of ionospheric perturbations is essential for the reliable operation of trans-ionospheric radio systems such as Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), GNSS augmentation services, and space-based remote sensing.

Beyond the detection of disturbed conditions, users increasingly require quantitative information on the strength, spatial scale, and temporal evolution of ionospheric variability across low, mid, and high latitudes.

While ionospheric indices provide an efficient means of condensing complex plasma dynamics into actionable parameters, most established indices rely on ground-based GNSS observations and suffer from limited coverage over oceans and sparsely instrumented regions.

In this contribution, we present recent advances in space-based ionospheric gradient indices derived from the ESA Swarm constellation, with a focus on their relevance for ionospheric monitoring and forecast-oriented applications.

Two ionospheric indices — the electron density gradient index (NeGIX), based on in-situ Langmuir probe measurements, and the TEC gradient Index (TEGIX), derived from Swarm GNSS Precise Orbit Determination data — have been part of the Swarm operational product suite since early 2025.

By exploiting the near-parallel orbits of Swarm satellites A and C, these indices quantify horizontal plasma gradients at medium spatial scales ( 30─200 km) and resolve both meridional and zonal components in the topside ionosphere.

Although the Swarm products are not yet available in near-real-time, recent improvements in data dissemination have reduced the effective latency to approximately 8 hours, significantly enhancing their applicability for low-latency monitoring, post-event analysis, and the validation of forecast and nowcast models.

Using more than a decade of Swarm observations, we summarize validation results for quiet conditions, seasonal climatology, and severe geomagnetic storms, including recent extreme events of Solar Cycle 25.
The indices robustly capture key ionospheric structures such as the equatorial ionization anomaly dynamics, mid-latitude ionization fronts, and high-latitude patchy perturbations.

During major storms, NeGIX and TEGIX reveal strong amplification, latitudinal expansion, and pronounced asymmetries of ionospheric gradients, providing quantitative measures of perturbation intensity and spatial extent across different latitude regimes.
Comparisons with established ground-based indices (e.g. GIX) demonstrate consistency, while highlighting the unique contribution of space-based gradients in regions lacking dense GNSS coverage.

We discuss how these Swarm-based ionospheric gradient indices complement existing ground-based methods and provide a space-based relevant database for ionospheric models, studies of perturbation propagation, and the development of future index-based approaches toward forecasting ionospheric disturbances.
In this context, these Swarm gradient indices represent a valuable bridge between scientific characterization and emerging operational needs in space weather monitoring and prediction.

title: The May 2024 Event versus the 2003 Halloween Storm

sentences.text: The geomagnetic storm of May 2024 served as a forceful reminder of how solar dynamics directly control Earth's magnetosphere.
This event triggered significant magnetic field fluctuations and visible auroral displays even at mid-latitudes.
Our study provides a systematic assessment between the 2003 Halloween storm and the May 2024 storm-the two most powerful geomagnetic events recorded over the last three solar cycles.
We analyze the solar conditions preceding each storm, specifically focusing on the characteristics of solar flares and halo Coronal Mass Ejections.
A comparative analysis of solar wind parameters and geomagnetic field data is conducted to quantify the intensity of each event and identify unique versus shared characteristics.
To evaluate geoeffectiveness, we discuss Geomagnetically Induced Current (GIC) index.
Notably, this work presents the first GIC index calculations for the May 2024 event, utilizing data from the European region spanning latitudes 58°-70°.

While the 2003 Halloween storm GIC impacts are well-documented, this work presents the first systematic calculation of GIC indices for the May 2024 event using the same methodology, allowing for a one-to-one comparison of induction risk.

title: Critical Ground-Based Instruments For the Study of GICs

sentences.text: Space weather causes geomagnetic disturbances that can affect critical infrastructure.
Understanding the dynamic response of the coupled solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere system to severe space weather is essential for mitigation purposes.

Unfortunately, one of the major challenges to our understanding of the M-I coupling processes is the limited availability of ground-based instruments, such as magnetometers, all-sky imagers, and more.
In this study, we focus on ground-based instruments that are critical to the study of geomagnetically induced currents (GICs).
We show the evolution of various networks and discuss the future needs that will advance our understanding of GICs characteristics and drivers.

title: Space Weather Canada: Recent Advances in Monitoring

sentences.text: Canada has a complex magnetic environment and is among the countries most affected by space weather.

With a long history of magnetic field observations, the government run network of geomagnetic observatories is operated by the Canadian Hazards Information Service (CHIS), Natural Resources Canada (NRCan).
Currently, the network consists of 14 active stations which cover polar cap, auroral and sub-auroral latitudes and provide real time data used for monitoring and forecasting of geomagnetic activity.

While the space weather community uses various geomagnetic activity indices, such as the widely used 3-hour planetary K-index (Kp), for over 40 years Space Weather Canada (CHIS, NRCan) uses an hourly range index (HR) to describe local geomagnetic conditions across Canada.
This index is based on ranges of horizontal magnetic field components during each UT hour.
Recently, we undertook modernization of the geomagnetic forecast and explored improvements in the Canadian indices and activity scales.
This includes potential use of a running-hourly range (rHR) index, which is based on ranges of horizontal components in a sliding one hour interval window.
This sliding window can take minute steps and is better suited for real time geomagnetic activity monitoring.
Moreover, the rHR index can better capture the magnitude of magnetic field variations than the HR index.
Here, we examine data from the geomagnetic observatory network for 1973-2025, compare HR and rHR indices, and perform statistical analysis of activity to improve the geomagnetic activity scale.

Geomagnetic activity monitoring and forecasting has been a cornerstone of Space Weather Canada's work since 1970s, particularly in the aftermath of the March 1989 geomagnetic storm and the Hydro-Québec blackout.
During the last decade significant efforts were undertaken to include and expand monitoring of ionospheric conditions.

Over the last two decades, the CHIS network has expanded to include riometers to monitor ionospheric absorption and degradation in High-Frequency (HF) communications, and more recently Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers to monitor ionospheric scintillations.
Densification of the riometer and GNSS receiver network is ongoing across the country.
Here, we report on the development of regional disturbance indicators that characterize ionospheric activity as it pertains to absorption and scintillation.

title: Ground-Based Observations and Modelling of Geomagnetically Induced Currents During the January 2026 Storm

sentences.text: Geomagnetic disturbances (GMDs) associated with solar storms can produce large geoelectric fields at Earth's surface, driving near-DC currents through the conductive ground and long infrastructure such as power transmission networks.

These geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) are of particular concern for electric power systems because they can cause half-cycle transformer saturation, excessive heating, voltage instability, and, in extreme cases, widespread service disruption.

A unique academia─industry collaboration among the University of Alberta, AltaLink L.P., ATCO Electric, and the Alberta Electric System Operator has established an integrated ground-based observational and modelling framework to investigate GICs in Alberta, Canada.

We combine transformer neutral-to-ground GIC measurements, high-resolution magnetometer observations, geoelectric field modelling using three-dimensional Earth conductivity structure, and a detailed DC equivalent power grid model.
During the geomagnetic storm of January 19-20, 2026, the peak measured GIC reached ∼75

A/phase in central Alberta, exceeding the ∼55 A/phase recorded at the same substation during the more globally intense May 2024 superstorm, despite the latter having a substantially stronger storm-time disturbance index.

This comparison demonstrates that the spatio-temporal scale of the GMD, geoelectric field orientation, subsurface conductivity, and power network topology jointly affect the GIC flowing through a given portion of the electric power network.
We observe that across multiple geomagnetic storms, some of the largest measured GICs occur consistently in central Alberta.
At the same time, modelling indicates similarly elevated GIC in northeastern Alberta, reflecting strong influence by geophysical factors and network topology.

We further evaluate an operational grid reconfiguration implemented immediately before the start of the January 2026 storm - reconnection of a high-voltage transmission line serving northern Alberta - to assess its influence on GIC through comparative simulations.

These results highlight the critical role of coordinated ground-based observation and modelling in characterizing regional space-weather risk, demonstrating how data-driven analysis can support operational mitigation strategies for power-grid resilience.

title: Potential impact of space weather effects on the variability in selected parameters characterizing Polish National Power System during the geomagnetic storm of 14 November 2012

sentences.text: We analyze the moderate geomagnetic storm of 14 November 2012 potential impact on the variability in selected parameters characterizing Polish National Power System.
We utilize anonymized, standardized hourly transmission data with the solar wind and heliospheric parameters with the geomagnetic indices.
Cross-correlation methods revealed the strongest correlation, r = 0.74, between a current-harmonic component and the Dst-index at a lag of −8 hours.
The most noticeable anti-correlation, with r = −0.66, occurred between current harmonics and the Ap-index at lags of −9 to −11 hours during a storm interval that reached minimal values of Dst-index.
Principal Component Analysis and Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering demonstrated that seven principal components captured almost 90% of the variance.
Our results indicated that moderate storms can match with measureable changes in power-transfer and harmonic-related parameters of power system, underlining the need for multi-event studies.
This investigation proves that space weather may contribute to observable variability in the Polish power network.

title: The SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS) onboard the Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) spacecraft: The newest solar wind particle capability of the United States Space Weather Program

abbreviations.SOLAR-1: Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1

sentences.text: The Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) spacecraft is the newest space weather satellite of the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
It was launched on September 24, 2025, and it is currently stationed in a stable orbit around the Sun-Earth Lagrange 1 (L1) point.
It is planned to become operational in the spring of 2026.
It is designed to deliver real-time observations of the solar corona to help improve forecasts of solar events that can impact Earth.

These include coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and other plasma structures emanating from the solar atmosphere, as well as the geomagnetic storms resulting from the interaction of CMEs with the Earth's magnetosphere.
The storms may induce numerous space weather effects, including power grid outages, satellite communication disruptions, and radiation harmful to humans in space.
One of the instruments onboard SOLAR-1 is the SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS).
STIS has two telescopes, one for electrons and one for ions, both equipped with solid state detectors that measure electrons in the range 25-250 keV, and ions in the range 25-6000 keV.
Both telescopes have an 80° x 60° Field-of-View (FOV) pointing at 50° from the Sun direction, on the ecliptic and along the Parker spiral.
The main purpose of STIS is to measure gradual Energetic Ion Enhancements (EIEs) that result from solar wind plasma acceleration by an interplanetary shock as it propagates out from the Sun.

The Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) monitors the flux enhancements at 47-68 keV in order to provide an advance warning of an incoming geomagnetic storm (several hours to a day), as opposed to the actual detection of the shock at L1 in the magnetic field and plasma, which gives only 10s of minutes of advanced warning.

The STIS data products consist of differential particle fluxes with 2-s cadence plus 1-min averages provided by NOAA's National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI) and used for space weather alerts by SWPC.
In this presentation we discuss the calibration/validation steps taken to ensure accurate and reliable STIS products for operational and scientific use.

title: Prediction of Significant Solar Flares Using Bidirectional LSTMS

sentences.text: Accurate solar flare prediction is important because major flares can cause serious damage to space-based and Earth-based infrastructure, including satellites, communication systems, navigation services, and power grids.
However, predicting major solar flares using Artificial Intelligence (AI) is challenging because such events are rare and the magnetic fields of active regions (AR) evolve in complex ways.

This work introduces a solar magnetic dataset covering the years 2010 to 2025 that enforces strict AR consistency over time, reducing cross-region leakage present in many existing flare forecasting pipelines.
We compare classical machine learning models trained on 72-hour summary statistics with a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) model that uses full 72-hour magnetic field sequences.
While the baseline models show high specificity but very low flare recall, the active region-grouped sequence model achieves much higher sensitivity.
On a chronologically separated test set from 2021 to 2025, the model achieves a True Skill Statistic (TSS) of 0.446 and a flare recall of 0.690 at an optimised decision threshold.
These results demonstrate the importance of AR-consistent temporal modelling and provide a clean, reproducible benchmark dataset for future solar flare forecasting studies.
The curated dataset and code are publicly available to support operational development

title: Organizational Specifics of Geoinduced Current Monitoring for Saturated Magnetic System of Power Transformer

sentences.text: This paper substantiates the monitoring of power transformer operation with a magnetic system saturated under the action of geoinduced currents (GIC).
The authors identify the requirements for the integration of the GIC monitoring system for the saturated magnetic system of a power transformer with the emergency event recorder.
GIC recording start and end conditions were set for the saturated magnetic system of a power transformer.
A structural diagram was developed, and key technical specifications were identified for the integrated GIC monitoring system.
The identification criteria for the magnetic system saturation due to GIC were set.
The key parameters were identified for the filter block of the GIC monitoring system: the low-pass filter and the strip filter.

The local GIC monitoring system using an autonomous emergency event recorder shall help prevent power transformer damage due to GIC and reduce the number of emergency shutdowns in the power grid during geomagnetic storms.

title: GIC Modeling for a Three-Phase, Three-Limb Transformer: Line-Resistance Sensitivity

sentences.text: Geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) caused by solar storms in the form of geomagnetic disturbances (GMDs) are a global phenomenon and can strike power systems at any time.
The likelihood of such events increases with solar flare and sunspot activity, which is nearing its cyclical peak.
A nonlinear MATLAB─Simscape model of a three-phase, three-limb transformer operating at no load is developed to assess how small winding-resistance variations influence GIC effects.
The model captures core nonlinearity, limb coupling, and inherent core asymmetry, while GIC is emulated via neutral dc injection (200 A).

Under GIC, a modest +5% resistance increase applied to any single phase reshapes magnetizing current waveforms and elevates harmonic content and total harmonic distortion (THD), even when the core is idealized as symmetric.
When realistic core asymmetry is included, the same resistance perturbations amplify waveform distortion further, revealing a coupled sensitivity to both electrical imbalance and magnetic geometry.
These results indicate that resistance imbalance whether from manufacturing tolerances, temperature drift, or aging can materially affect system performance under high-GIC events.
The findings motivate routine, temperature-corrected resistance monitoring over time and GIC studies that incorporate measured limb asymmetry when setting harmonic limits and protection thresholds.

title: Solar Flare Prediction and Intensity Estimation Using a Multi-Task Transformer Encoder

sentences.text: GPS navigation, High Frequency communications, and Automated Dependent Surveillance (ADSB) are adversely impacted by solar flare activity on Earth.

A dual output transformer network has been developed that predicts the occurrence and intensity of solar flares based on sequences of magnetograms (the graphical representation of the magnetic field around the Sun).
By employing the multi-head self attention mechanism to model the behavior of the solar magnetic field, time-dependent patterns in the solar magnetic field data are effectively captured.

The experimental results demonstrate that M-class solar flares can be forecast and Xray flux can be estimated, which will allow aviation authorities to make decisions regarding/reallocate flight frequencies, provide back-up navigation, and issue Transpolar Route advisories.
For operational space weather applications, the transformer architecture outperforms conventional forecasting and machine learning methods.

title: Geo-Coordinate Based Solar Flare Impact Prediction on Submarine Cables Using Hybrid XGBoost-ML Algorithm

sentences.text: Global connectivity is heavily reliant on submarine fibre optic cables to connect users worldwide; however, submarine fibre optic cables face the risk of being disrupted through geomagnetic disturbances caused by extreme weather events which is solar flares (Solar-induced geomagnetic disturbances) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs).These Solar flares and CMEs create geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) that can affect the infrastructure of submarine fibre optic cables.

In this study, we present a novel hybrid geo-spatial AI system using a combination of Gradient Boosting algorithms to classify solar flares and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) to predict the risk level of the cable to disruptions from the GICs caused by solar flares and CMEs.

By incorporating feature sets of geomagnetism and geographic co-ordinates, the proposed system converts the complex parameters of space weather into actionable risk categories at an infrastructure level.

title: Complex Observation of the Ionosphere for Enhanced Satellite Trajectory Planning

sentences.text: The operation of space-based assets is increasingly threatened by various forms of space weather, leading to significant disruptions in satellite functionality.

These anomalies are primarily driven by solar phenomena such as Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), High-Speed Solar Winds (HSS), and Solar Proton Events (SPEs), which acutely affect satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
The enhanced neutral density associated with thermospheric heating can increase satellite drag, accelerate orbital decay, and require more frequent reboost maneuvers.
Mitigating these risks requires reliable information on coupled ionosphere-thermosphere disturbances.

This study proposes an integrated methodology that combines multi-source ground and space-based data to construct a real-time 3D representation of the ionosphere, ultimately outputting a dynamic 4D model for effective satellite trajectory planning.
By blending localized Very Low Frequency (VLF) waveguide soundings with multi-mission satellite data assimilation, this framework establishes a robust tracking engine for space weather mitigation.

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Space Weather Effects on Internet Performance and GNSS Reliability

sentences.text: Space phenomena such as solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar wind variations, geomagnetic disturbances, and ionospheric irregularities often have direct effects on Earth's communication networks.
These effects mainly include degradation of internet performance and inaccuracies in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS).

This paper proposes a machine-learning framework that helps to predict the effects of these space weather on internet latency, packet loss, Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routing stability, and GNSS positioning accuracy.
The system takes space weather observations from NASA and NOAA and combines them with geospatial data which is fed as inputs to machine-learning models to predict the risks.
A dashboard analysis is also provided which helps with visualising effects on a colour-coded world map, time-series trends and solar weather timeline.
The results demonstrate the feasibility of forecasting space weather-induced disruptions using a machinelearning framework.

title: Mitigating the Impact of Geomagnetically-Induced Currents on Transformer Differential Protection

sentences.text: Faults within the transformer protection zone must be promptly cleared to prevent system instability and equipment damage.
However, geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) can cause transformer saturation and harmonic distortion, leading to misoperation or desensitization of differential protection schemes.
This paper evaluates the effectiveness of waveshape-based unblocking as an auxiliary function to enhance the sensitivity and dependability of transformer differential protection under GIC conditions.

A hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) setup was used, incorporating a commercial relay and a validated 500/230 kV transformer model connected to a reduced equivalent of Dominion Energy Virginia's transmission grid.

Through 2,322 real-time simulations across various fault types, fault resistances, and GIC magnitudes, the study demonstrates that waveshape-based unblocking significantly improves fault detection and reduces clearing time during geomagnetic disturbances.
The results support the adoption of waveshape-based unblocking in transformers exposed to elevated GIC levels.

title: Dynamic Modeling, Selection, and Placement of Mitigation Devices for HEMP/GMD Events

sentences.text: A high-altitude electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) or solar-geomagnetic disturbance (GMD) can drive low-frequency geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) that force large power transformers into saturation, distorting AC waveforms, increasing losses, and risking thermal damage.

This paper develops dynamic models of large synthetic grids that capture the transient response to simulated HEMP insults, then applies multi-objective optimization to quantify the trade-off between mitigation-device type, placement, and resulting transformer saturation.

The study shows that flux-blocking devices provide the steepest reduction in relative saturation for a given device count, and that incorporating cost weights enables analysis of trade-offs between competing mitigation technologies and deployment strategies.

title: Design and Simulation of a Hybrid-Solid State Transformer with HEMP/GMD Mitigation Capabilities

sentences.text: A high-altitude electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) or naturally occurring geomagnetic disturbance (GMD) has the potential to impact electric power grids by inducing low-frequency common-mode (CM) currents.
When these currents flow through grounded power transformers, they can drive the transformer core into magnetic saturation, degrading performance and potentially causing system failures.
This work introduces a hybrid solid-state transformer (H-SST) that integrates a conventional magnetic transformer with a power-electronic-based solid state transformer.
The proposed H-SST mitigates the harmful effects of HEMP/GMD-induced currents, thus enhancing grid resilience.

Additionally, the H-SST also provides operational capabilities to the grid, including power factor correction, voltage regulation, and a fail-normal mode that ensures continued load service even if the power electronics malfunction.
An overview of the H-SST architecture, power electronics, and control strategy is presented, and its performance is evaluated across normal and abnormal HEMP/GMD grid scenarios.

title: Analysis of High-Latitude Total Electron Content and Scintillation during Recent Geomagnetic Storms

abbreviations.MACAWS: Monitors for Alaskan and Canadian Auroral Weather in Space
abbreviations.INGV: Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia
abbreviations.ROTI: rate of change of TEC index

sentences.text: Solar cycle 25 began in December 2019, and since there have been a significant number of major geomagnetic storms, including the large May 2024 storm, known as the Gannon storm, the October 2024 storm, as well as more recent storms in January and June 2025.
As we are approaching, or are now in, the declining phase of this cycle, more geomagnetic storms are anticipated.
We will review and compare the seasonal, hemispheric, and geomagnetic dependencies of the storms in this solar cycle, focusing on observations from the mid-to-high latitudes.
For example, how often and where do we observe the storm enhanced density feature and how does it compare to those observed in solar cycle 23 and 24.
We will also focus on the hemispheric differences observed in both the total electron content (TEC), differential TEC, and the quantity of scintillation observed in each hemisphere.

We will utilize data in the Madrigal database including the TEC observations from the global ground-based network of GNSS receivers and scintillation statistics obtained from networks of specialized GNSS receivers.

These networks include: the NSF MRI Collaborative: Development of Monitors for Alaskan and Canadian Auroral Weather in Space (MACAWS), the Canadian High Arctic Scintillation Network (CHAIN), the Low-Latitude Ionospheric Sensor Network (LISN), and in the Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia (INGV) network.

In addition, starting this year, we have been computing statistics for the rate of change of TEC index (ROTI) using all of the GNSS receivers that we routinely process (>5000 globally distributed receivers).
ROTI is a proxy index for scintillation.
We are now extending this processing to also include the major geomagnetic storm periods in 2023-2024.
We will describe the advantages and disadvantages of this index.

title: Ionospheric Dynamics and Its Impact on RF Applications During Superstorm Events

sentences.text: Modern technological systems, including those underpinning the global economy, are increasingly dependent on radio frequency (RF) communication systems - both ground-based and satellite-based.
Consequently, the need for reliable and resilient RF systems, particularly those providing precise positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services, has never been more critical.
However, the accuracy of RF systems can be compromised by both man-made issues - such as radio frequency interference - and natural disturbances like geomagnetic storms.

These storms alter the characteristics and distribution of ionospheric density, which can significantly affect RF propagation and disrupt applications, such as SATCOM communications and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) navigation services.

In this paper, we investigate the impact of geomagnetic storm events occurring in May, August, and October 2024 on the performance of GNSS applications for users across low-, mid-, and high-latitude regions.
We utilize multi-instrument observations to identify the drivers and characterize the ionospheric disturbances during these events.
In particular, we assess the similarities and differences in the levels of ionospheric disturbances and its spatial distribution during these storm events.

Particularly, we examine the latitudinal distribution of these disturbances to determine whether the impacts are significant even in mid-latitudes, regions that are traditionally considered relatively calm.

title: Expanding GNSS Ground-Based Ionospheric Monitoring: Retrieving Absolute TEC from Low-Elevation Wideband Signals During May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm Period

sentences.text: Accurate estimation of ionospheric total electron content (TEC) is essential for improving global navigation satellite system (GNSS) performance and understanding space weather.
Our work investigates the use of wideband GNSS pseudorange data to recover low-elevation absolute TEC measurements, which are typically discarded due to high noise and multipath.
Wideband signals like GPS L5 offer improved code resolution and reduced noise, making them promising for single-frequency TEC retrieval.
Expanding the use of low-elevation wideband GNSS signals addresses a key limitation in ionospheric monitoring.
Conventional GNSS-based TEC observations often exclude signals below$15-30^{\circ}$elevation due to multipath and low SNR, resulting in substantial data loss.
This is particularly problematic in high-latitude regions, where ground-based receiver coverage is sparse and satellite visibility at high elevations is limited.
Our past work shows that noise in wideband pseudorange-derived TEC is significantly lower than that of narrowband signals, especially below 30° elevation.
However, hardware biases, a nuisance error in this process, need to be removed in order to retrieve absolute (unbiased) TEC.

title: CLARE: Classification-based Regression for Electron Temperature Prediction

sentences.text: Electron temperature is a fundamental parameter governing the state and variability of the upper atmosphere and near-Earth space environment.
It strongly affects the forces exerted by the pressure gradient and the ambipolar electric field, which play critical roles in driving plasmasphere refilling, ion outflow, and the polar wind.

Despite its importance, electron temperature has historically been underexplored in the context of machine learning (ML) - based space-weather prediction, mainly due to the scarcity of global observation data.

In this work, we present CLARE, a machine-learning model developed to predict electron temperature in the Earth's plasmasphere by leveraging measurements from JAXA's AKEBONO (EXOS-D) satellite combined with solar and geomagnetic activity indices.
CLARE employs a classification-based regression approach that discretizes the continuous electron temperature space into 150 intervals.
By framing the prediction task as classification, the model achieves higher accuracy skill while naturally providing an estimate of predictive uncertainty.
Compared with a standard regression approach, this CLARE framework yields a$6.46 \%$improvement in prediction accuracy.

On an independent AKEBONO test set, CLARE attains$69.67 \%$accuracy within$10 \%$of ground truth, and during a known moderate geomagnetic-storm interval (January 31─February 7, 1991), the model maintains$46.17 \%$accuracy.
These results highlight the model's robustness under both geomagnetically quiet and disturbed conditions.
This study highlights the need for future missions to make further electron temperature measurements, which remain limited in spatial coverage.

Furthermore, beyond immediate electron temperature prediction, this study demonstrates that advanced machine-learning architectures, applied to long-term, publicly available satellite datasets, can substantially enhance space-weather modeling capabilities.
Reliable electron temperature forecasts will improve the fidelity of next-generation operational space-weather forecasting systems, with broad implications for mitigating spacecraft charging.

title: Response of High-Latitude GNSS Scintillations to Ionospheric Gradients and Particle Precipitation During Storms and Substorms

sentences.text: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are highly susceptible to ionospheric scintillations, which can degrade positioning accuracy by several meters even under mild conditions and can cause total signal loss during periods of strong geomagnetic activity.

High-latitude regions are particularly affected due to enhanced particle precipitation and strong ionospheric convection, making these areas critical for both operational navigation systems and space weather forecasting.

This study examines the response of global scintillations during geomagnetic storms and substorms, using eight years (2013─2021) of amplitude (S4) and phase ($\sigma_{\phi}$) measurements from the Canadian High Arctic Ionospheric Network (CHAIN), providing extensive coverage across multiple geomagnetic latitudes and local times.
We find that scintillation response is largest during the storm main phase and the substorm expansion phase, highlighting the key role of transient geomagnetic activity.

The analysis considers all storm and substorm phases to characterize how temporal and spatial gradients of total electron content (TEC), together with particle precipitation, are linked to scintillations.

Statistical analysis, considering response times up to one hour after storm and substorm onsets, reveals significant correlations between TEC gradients and the$\sigma_{\phi}$index, particularly near dawn and noon magnetic local time at 70° magnetic latitude.
The response shifts poleward with increasing response time and exhibits discernible dawn─dusk asymmetries.
In addition, a persistent response develops in the convection throat, becoming noticeable after 10 minutes and possibly associated with polar cap patches and cusp precipitation.
Enhancement of scintillations is also observed at premidnight, likely associated with monoenergetic electron precipitation.

The observed density fluctuations that drive scintillations are likely generated by gradient drift instabilities in regions of strong convection, with Kelvin─Helmholtz instabilities potentially contributing in areas of strong flow shear.

The spatial distribution further suggests that diffuse electron precipitation contributes to dawn─dusk asymmetries, whereas enhanced electron density in the convection throat during storms likely drives the noon response.

By systematically linking TEC gradients, particle precipitation, and observed scintillation responses, this study provides new insight into the physical mechanisms controlling GNSS signal disturbances at high latitudes and their temporal evolution, with implications for both operational navigation systems and predictive space weather modeling.
